p.note: : in class. Lat. when urbs or oppidum precedes the name of the place a prep. is used in preference to the simple local ablative (Kühner-Stegmann, i 480). Suetonius uses ortus (a) with ex, e.g. Tib. 1, 1, gens Claudia orta est ex Regillis oppido Sabinorum; (b) with a, e.g. Iul. 6, 1, maternum genus a regibus ortum; (c) with simple abl., e.g. Ner. 28, 1, regio genere ortam: Aug. 2, 3, equestri familia ortum se.

: cf. Tac. H. ii 50, origo illi e municipio Ferentio. Ferentium, or Ferentinum, was an Etruscan city on the site of the modern ruins of Ferento. It is mentioned again in Vesp. 3, and is to be distinguished from Ferentinum in the territory of the Hernici in Latium. It was probably a dependency of Volsinii in Etruscan times (Dennis, Cities and Cemeteries of Etruria, i³ 156 sqq.). We first hear of it in the time of Augustus as a Roman colony of small importance (Strab. v 226; Frontin. de colon.); Vitruvius (ii 7), like Tacitus, calls it a municipium. possessed a temple of Fortuna (Tac. A. xv 53), probably the Etruscan goddess Nurtia. There are the remains of a magnificent theatre at Ferento. The connexion of the family of Otho with Ferentium is confirmed by an inscription found there: M. Sal[vio Othoni Aug.] tribu[nic(ia) potest(ate)] municipe[s ... See Pauly-Wissowa, i A. 2035. It

: cf. Hor. C. iii 29, 1, where Maecenas is addressed as “Tyrrhena regum progenies," his ancestors on his father's side, the Cilnii, being Lucumones or chieftains at Arretium. Etruria in ancient times was a confederation of twelve states or cities, each with an aristocratic form of government, the chief rulers, who combined political and ecclesiastical functions, being called Lucumones; see Dennis, op. cit. i³ Introd. p. li.

: restored by Stephanus for “Silvius." Salvius, which is often found as a praenomen in the contracted form Sa. or Sal., did not become widespread as a gentile name till a late period. Those who bore it as a single name in Republican times were persons of no great distinction, often slaves e.g. the leader of the Sicilian slave war in 104: the influential freedman of Caesar often mentioned in Cicero's Letters: the literary slave or freedman of Atticus. The Salvius who as trib. pleb. in 43 B.C. vetoed the decree of the senate declaring Antony a public enemy and who later sided with Cicero against Antony and perished in the proscription may have been a kinsman of the M. Salvius Otho whom Suetonius mentions here; see Münzer in Pauly-Wissowa, i A. 2023.

: Suetonius is fond of introducing disjunctive questions depending on incertum or dubium, or with incertum and dubium omitted; e.g. Iul. 18, 1, profectus est incertum metune iudicii an quo maturius sociis subveniret: Iul. 58, 1, dubium cautior an audentior: Galb. 12, 3, illa quoque verene an falso per ludibrium iactabantur: Vesp. 1, 2, Flavius Petro bello civili Pompeianarum partium centurio an evocatus profugit. In our passage the first part of the interrogation is omitted. ..
: wife of Augustus; see on Galb. 1 and 5, 2. Galba was said to have owed his consulship to her (Galb. 2, 1, n.).
: similarly Titus was brought up along with Britannicus son of the emperor Claudius (Tit. 2, n.).

: by imperial favour a person of equestrian rank could become a senator in two ways: (1) the emperor could exercise his right of adlectio and admit him directly to the senate, assigning him a definite place on the roll, usually inter tribunicios, occasionally inter praetorios, and in the 3rd cent. even inter consulares, entitling him to the privileges of those who had actually filled these offices; (2) the emperor could bestow on him the latus clavus qualifying him to start with the vigintivirate (see on Galb. 6, 1) and then proceed to the quaestorship and the successive magistracies in the cursus honorum; sometimes the latus clavus cum quaestura was granted and then the imperial favourite could begin his career with the quaestorship, an office carrying with it admission to the senate. Cf. Mommsen, Staatsr. ii 938 sqq.

: this fact is mentioned by Tacitus also, who says that the emperor Otho had an “avus praetorius” (H. ii 50). By a curious coincidence the grandfather of Galba never went beyond being praetor; cf. Galb. 3, 3, avus non egressus praeturae gradum. On coins with the head of Augustus (Eckhel, v 289) this M. Salvius Otho is named as IIIvir A.A.A.F.F. (i.e. triumvir auro argento aere flando feriundo, one of the triumviri monetales, directors of the mint). For nec (= neque vero, neque tamen) cf. Oth. 5, 2 sollicitati reliqui, nec adeo multi; Dom. 7, 2, edixit, nec exsequi rem perseveravit.

div.p: §2. pater: Tac. H. ii 50, (Othoni) pater consularis; he was consul suffectus in 33 A.D., Galba being consul ordinarius during the first six months of that year (Galb. 6, 1). In the acta Arvalia (Henzen p. xlviii) this Lucius Otho is mentioned as "flamen et pro magistro" of the Fratres Arvales in 39 A.D. (Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 166).

p.note: : Hofstee conjectures that the mother belonged to the gens Titia and that her grandson Titianus (see below) derived his name from his grandmother, after the fashion of the period.

: “connexions"; cf. Nep. Dion 1, 2, Dion autem, praeter nobilem propinquitatem, generosamque maiorum famam, multa alia ab natura habuit bona; for the pl. cf. Cic. Fin. v 23, si propinquitates summo bono non continentur. Suetonius uses the word only here and in Ner. 35, 4; elsewhere necessitudo and necessitudines, the latter frequently in a concrete sense (= necessarii, ἀναγκαῖοι).

: absimilis (ἀνόμοιος, late Gr. ἀφόμοιος) is found once in class. Lat., Caes. B.G. iii 14, falces .. non absimili forma muralium falcium (sc. formae); it is always used with a negative (by litotes) and it takes the dative, as in Dom. 10, 1, arte formaque non absimilis magistro. ..

: there was a similar scandal current about Drusus (father of the emperor Claudius), who was borne by Livia three months after her marriage to Augustus, and it was said that Augustus had begotten him in adulterous intercourse with her while she was the wife of Tib. Claudius Nero (Claud. 1, fuit suspicio ex vitrico per adulterii consuetudinem procreatum). Suetonius uses plerique not merely in the sense of plurimi but also in that of multi or permulti (e.g. Galb. 16, 1; Dom. 6, 2:8, 2:10,5:19; so in Nep., Liv., Tac.); sometimes, as here, it is impossible to determine in which sense he is using it. The same difficulty presents itself in Tacitus; see Gerber and Greef, Lex. Tac.
: i.e. the offices included in the regular cursus honorum, the quaestorship, aedileship or tribuneship, praetorship, and consulship.

: held also by Galba (Galb. 7, 1), Vitellius (Vitell. 5), and Vespasian (Vesp. 4, 3). The provinces of Africa and Asia were reserved for consulares (see on “proconsulatum,” Galb. 3, 4). Lucius Otho probably succeeded Galba as proconsul and, like Galba, may have been invested with special military powers (see on Galb. 7, 1).

: we have no information as to the precise nature of these, or the province or provinces in which Lucius Otho held them. For an example of a provincial governor who was given an ‘“ extraordinarium imperium” see on Vitell. 2, 4, Lucius Syriae praepositus.

: in the division of provinces in 27 B.c. Illyricum was made a senatorial province, but in consequence of continual rebellions and the necessity of keeping a military force there it was transferred to the emperor (c. 10 B.c.) and divided into two provinces, Pannonia and Dalmatia. In a wider sense Illyricum included Noricum and Moesia.

: the name of this Camillus is variously recorded as Furius Camillus Scribonianus, L. Arruntius Camillus Scribonianus, Camillus Arruntius, Camillus Scribonianus, etc. Mommsen (Hermes iii 133 sqq.) shows that he was a son of M. Furius Camillus (cons. '8 A.D.); and was adopted by L. Arruntius (cons. 6 A.D.); his mother was the daughter of Scribonia and Sextus Pompeius, hence he was called Scribonianus. He was consul in 32 A.D. (see Oth. 2, 1), and was appointed governor (legatus Aug. pro. pr. consularis) of Dalmatia under Caligula. He was continued in this office under Claudius, but in 42 A.D. revolted against the emperor and announced that he would restore the republic. Many senators and knights flocked to him, but his soldiers refused to follow him and he was forced to flee to the island of Issa in the Adriatic where he killed himself according to Dio (lx 15, ἑκούσιος ἀπέθανε), but Tacitus (H. ii 75) says he was slain by a private soldier. See also Tac. H. i 89, A. xii 52; Plin. Ep. iii 16; Oros. vii 6.

: cf. Claud. 13, 2, bellum civile movit Furius Camillus Scribonianus Dalmatiae legatus, verum intra quintum diem oppressus est, legionibus quae sacramentum mutaverant in paenitentiam religione ('superstition'") conversis, postquam, denuntiato ad novum imperatorem itinere, casu quodam ac divinitus neque aquila ornari neque signa convelli moverique potuerunt.
: causal, see on Tit. 5, 1.
: no example of this construction (for the usual defectio ab) is given in the Thesaur. Ling. Lat.

: the use of the prep. ante shows that principia (= ἀρχεῖα, cf. Plut. Galb. 12, ἐν τοῖς ἀρχείοις, ἃ πριγκίπια καλοῦσι ῾Ρωμαῖοι) is here used for the officers' quarters themselves; it was also used in a wider sense for the large open space in the centre of the camp containing the general's tent (praetorium) and those of the higher officers, the eagle and standards of the legion, and the raised platform (tribunal) where the general administered justice and addressed the troops. The exact meaning of principia and the precise relation between principia and praetorium have been much disputed, some identifying principia with the via principalis or main street (E. and W.) of the camp or at least with that part of it which the officers' tents or quarters adjoined. See Daremberg-Saglio, i 945, iv '640; Smith, Dict. Ant. i3 374. The principia and praetorium are often mentioned in connexion with military punishments of a merely degrading kind (see on Vitell. 8, 1), but executions usually took place outside the porta decumana of the camp and were supervised by the tribunes or centurions, so the procedure of Lucius Otho was quite exceptional.

: cf. Tac. H. ii 75, sic Scribonianum sub Claudio interfectum, sic percussorem eius Volaginium e gregario ad summa militiae provectum. The use of promovere aliquem in the sense of perducere, producere, provehere is post-Aug.

div.p: §3. detecta equitis R. fraude: this was presumably one (though we know not which) of the conspiracies by equites against Claudius which are mentioned by Suetonius, Tacitus, and Dio; cf. Suet. Claud. 13, reperti et equestris ordinis duo in publico cum dolone (“sword-cane'') ac venatorio cultro praestolantes, alter ut egressum theatro, alter ut sacrificantem apud Martis aedem adoreretur: Tac. A. xi 22 (47 A.D.), interea Romae, nullis palam neque cognitis mox causis, Cn. Nonius eques Romanus ferro accinctus reperitur in coetu salutantium principem; nam postquam tormentis dilaniabatur, de se non infitiatus conscios non edidit, incertum an occultans : Dio lx 18 (43 A.D.), καί τις ἐν τούτῳ τῶν ἱππέων, ὡς καὶ ἐπιβουλεύσας τῷ Κλαυδίῳ, κατὰ τοῦ Καπιτωλίου ὑπό τε τῶν δημάρχων (‘tribunes '') καὶ τῶν ὑπάτων (“consuls") κατεκρημνίσθη. Hofstee is probably right in assuming that Suetonius in the present passage is referring to the design against the life of Claudius which is mentioned by Tacitus as frustrated in 47 A.D., as L. Otho was ‘“inter patricios adlectus” when Claudius was censor in 48, and thus Otho's reward would come shortly after his service to the emperor. Dessau (Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 168) thinks that the reference is to the attempt in 43 which is mentioned by Dio.

p.note: : cf. Tit. 2. Nero conferred a like honour on Tigellinus and Nerva; Tac. A. xv 72, tum, quasi gesta bello expositurus, vocat senatum et triumphale decus Petronio Turpiliano consulari, Cocceio Nervae praetori designato, Tigellino praefecto praetorii tribuit, Tigellinum et Nervam ita extollens ut super triumphales in foro imagines apud Palatium quoque effigies eorum sisteret. In our passage and in Tac. l.c. Friedlaender (Sitteng. iii¹º 75) takes Palatium as the Palatine hill, not the imperial Palace; so too Hofstee, on the ground that in both cases the senate decrees the honour, and the senate had nothing to do with the Palace. But the erection of statues required the authorisation of the senate (Galb. 23 n.), and the emperors went through the formality of asking the senate to decree the statues.

: the creation of a large number of patricians by Claudius as censor in 48 A.D. is mentioned in Tac. A. xi 25, Isdem diebus, in numerum patriciorum adscivit Caesar vetustissimum quemque e senatu aut quibus clari parentes fuerant, paucis iam reliquis familiarum, quas Romulus maiorum et L. Brutus minorum gentium appellaverant, exhaustis etiam quas dictator Caesar lege Cassia et princeps Augustus lege Saenia sublegere; laetaque haec in rem publicam munia multo gaudio censoris inibantur. Under the Republic new patrician gentes were coopted by the patrician curiae in the comitia curiata; the dictator Caesar and Augustus created them under special law; Claudius created them in virtue of his powers as censor, so too Vespasian and Titus (see note on Vesp. 9, 2); when the censorship fell into abeyance, the emperors, beginning with Trajan, created them in virtue of their general powers. See Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 1100 sq., iii 29 sq. Vir, quo meliores, etc.: a similar eulogy was bestowed by Augustus on Drusus (father of the emperor Claudius) after his death: Claud. 1, 5, defunctum ita laudaverit, ut deos precatus sit, similes ei Caesares (i.e. Gaius and Lucius) suos facerent.

: Reid, on Cic. Balb. 9, points out the difference between “sperare” to look forward to what is practicable and “optare” to look forward to what can happen only by an extraordinary stroke of good fortune; optare is used of the wild dreams of philosophers, e.g. Cic. Acad. ii 121, somnia censet haec esse Democriti non docentis sed optantis.

: Tacitus does not mention her name, but he says of Otho, "pater consularis, avus praetorius; maternum genus inpar nec tamen indecorum” (H. ii 50). Eutropius (vii 17) says that the family of Otho's mother was more noble than that of his father: Otho materno genere nobilior quam paterno, neutro tamen obscuro (some would transpose paterno and materno, to make Eutropius accord with Tacitus). The notice of Otho in Suidas begins: ὁ μετὰ Γάλβαν βασιλεύσας, γένους ἀσήμου καὶ ἀφανοῦς ὤν (Barth proposed γένους μὴ ἀσήμου : cf. Plut. Galb. 19, Μάρκος Ὄθων, ἀνὴρ γένει μὲν οὐκ ἀφανής).

: it is generally assumed that she was of an equestrian family, the epithet splendidus being applied to an eques of high position and great wealth who had held no magisterial office at Rome (Mommsen, Staatsr. iii 565); but more probably the adj. here means simply "of distinguished family," the precise rank of the family being unspecified; cf. Tit. 4, 2, duxit uxorem Marciam Furnillam splendidi generis: Tac. Agr. 6, Domitiam Decidianam, splendidis natalibus ortam, sibi iunxit.
: for this expression see on Vesp. 3.

: his full name was Lucius Salvius Otho Titianus. Tacitus (A. xii 52), mentioning him as consul under Claudius in 52 A.D., calls him Salvius Otho, but in H. i 90 ii 60, Agr. 6 gives his name as Salvius Titianus. He is mentioned very often in the records of the Fratres Arvales from 57 to 69 A.D. (C.I.L. vi 2038-2051). He was proconsul of Asia ("in omnem aviditatem pronus," Tac. Agr. 6) with Agricola as his quaestor in 63-64, and became consul for a second time in 69 along with his brother the emperor. When Otho set out to meet Vitellius he left Titianus in charge of the city, but soon sent for him to take command of the army; he was defeated at Betriacum, where his army surrendered, but he was pardoned by the enemy, "pietate et ignavia excusatus" (Tac. H. ii 60).
: the future emperor, Marcus Salvius Otho.
: having the same cognomen Otho; in Vitell. 2, 2 “cognominis” means having the same nomen.

: Roman maidens might be betrothed when mere children; they were regarded as marriageable from the beginning of the thirteenth year, and were usually married between the ages of thirteen and sixteen, fourteen being the average age, though there were instances of girls being married when under twelve, e.g. Messalina was only eleven when she married the sixteen-year-old Nero; see the statistics on the subject given in Friedlaender, Sitteng. iv¹º 133 sqq.

: this son of Germanicus and Agrippina assumed the toga virilis in 23 A.D.; he and his elder brother Nero were designated as heirs and successors of Tiberius, but Sejanus, who was ambitious to reign, used Drusus as a tool to secure the banishment and death of Nero, and then worked the downfall of Drusus, who was accused of treason to the emperor and sentenced to death by the senate. Tiberius did not execute him at once, but kept him a prisoner in a vault of the palace for some years, and finally in 33 A.D. had him starved to death (Suet. Tib. 54, 65; Calig. 12; Tac. A. iv 4, 60; vi 23: Dio lviii 22).

: it is not known whether Drusus married this daughter of Lucius Otho, but we are told that in 30 A.D. he was already married to Aemilia Lepida (Dio lviii 3; Tac. A. vi 40, Aemilia Lepida, iuveni Druso nupta), who was a shameless character driven to suicide through her profligacy; she was amongst those who accused her husband to Tiberius.
: April 28 (32 A.D.).
: see on c. 1, 2.

: father of the emperor Nero, and husband of Agrippina daughter of Germanicus (see on Galb. 5, 1); after his consulship (32 A.D., see Vitell. 2, 2) he was proconsul of Sicily; accused of many crimes, adultery, incest, murder, he only escaped execution through the death of Tiberius; he died of dropsy (aqua intercus) in 37. Suetonius (Ner. 5) speaks of him as “omni parte vitae detestabilis," and says that when his friends congratulated him on the birth of Nero he replied that nothing that was not abominable and a public bane could be born of Agrippina and himself.

: Tac. H. i 13, Otho pueritiam incuriose, adulescentiam petulanter egerat: Plut. Galb. 19, Μάρκος Ὄθων .. τρυφῇ καὶ φιληδονίαις εὐθὺς ἐκ παίδων ἐν ὀλίγοις ῾Ῥωμαίων (“as few even of the Romans were") διεφθαρμένος.

: the flagrum or flagellum was a "knout" or "cat" of knotted cord or wire, the thongs being often loaded with pieces of metal or knuckle-bones. It was used for the punishment of slaves (Marquardt, Privatl.2 182).

: in post-Aug. writers obiurgare is often used of corporal chastisement; e.g. Suet. Calig. 20, ferulis obiurgari: Pers. v 169, nugaris; solea puer obiurgabere rubra: Petron. Satyr. 34, colaphis obiurgare puerum iussit: Sen. Ira iii 12, 6, servulum istum verberibus obiurga.

: assaults committed by revelling young "Mohocks" in the streets at night are often referred to by Plautus; e.g. Stich. 606, Non tu scis, quam adflictentur homines noctu hic in via: Trin. 315, ne noctu irem obambulatum, neu suum adimerem alteri: Amph. 153, Qui me alter est audacior homo aut quis confidentior, Iuventutis mores qui sciam, qui hoc noctis solus ambulem? Cf. Juv. iii 278 sqq. Nero was notorious for his nightly escapades (Ner. 26, Tac. A. xiii 25), as were also Caligula and Vitellius; cf. Capitol. L. Veri c. 4, in tantum vitiorum Gaianorum et Neronianorum ac Vitellianorum fuisse aemulum ut vagaretur nocte per tabernas ac lupanaria et comissaretur cum triconibus, committeret rixas, etc. ...

: “drunken"; cf. Apul. Met. iii 5, cum a cena me serius aliquanto reciperem potulentus. In Cicero potulenta means "drinkables." N.D. ii 56, 141, gustatus in ea parte oris, qua esculentis et potulentis iter natura patefecit; cf. Scaevola's definition of “penus," Gell. iv 1, 17, penus est quod esculentum et potulentum est. The termination -lentus denotes "full of" (e.g. fraudulentus, vinolentus, opulentus), and so potulentus more naturally means “full of drink" than "drinkable," and in Plin. N.H. viii 90 we find "esculentum os” where the meaning is 'filled with food."

: sagatio (Gr. παλμός) was the Roman parallel to our "tossing in a blanket" (Fr. berner, Germ. prellen, Fuchsprellen). Cf. Mart. i 3, 8, ibis ab excusso missus in astra sago; Libanius, orat. 58, 18. The use of the word sagum (a soldier's cloak, see Marquardt, Privatl.2 561, 565) shows that it was originally an amusement of the soldiers (cf. Friedlaender on Mart. l.c.).

: colere "to court the favour of, by showing deference to" is frequently distinguished from diligere “to love", e.g. Cic. Lael. 53, quis enim aut eum diligat, quem metuat, aut eum, a quo se metui putet? coluntur tamen simulatione dumtaxat ad tempus: Plin. Ep. ii 9, 6, diligeris, coleris, frequentaris: Sidon. Ep. iv 4, ipse hinc amplius capiebatur, quod se diligi magis quam quasi coli intelligebat: Mart. ii 55, Vis te, Sexte, coli: volebam amare. | Parendum est tibi: quod iubes, colere: | Sed si te colo, Sexte, non amabo.

: used adjectivally as in Ner. 11, 1, anus matronas. With the possible exception of Cic. Scaur. 8, uxorem, anum et locupletem et molestam, this adjectival use is limited to poetry and post-Aug. prose.
: this passage is quoted with a number of others by Mayor to illustrate Juv. i 38, in caelum quos evehit optima summi | nunc via processus, vetulae vesica beatae.

: Suetonius always uses insinuare in the passive (middle) and c. dat.; cf. Calig. 12, 2, insinuatus Macroni: Gramm. 21, Augusto insinuatus est Melissus: vit. Horat. 3, ac primo Maecenati, deinde Augusto insinuatus. In earlier writers, from Plautus onward, we find such phrases as insinuare se in familiaritatem (amicitiam) alicuius; insinuare se ad aliquem or alicui; and with the reflexive omitted insinuare alicui (e.g. Cic. de or. i 20, 90, blandiri suppliciter et subtiliter insinuare eis, a quibus, etc.).

: the friendship of Nero and Otho was a case of ὁ ὅμοιος τῷ ὁμοίῳ, pares cum paribus. Tacitus says the same thing, H. i 13, Otho gratus Neroni aemulatione luxus; cf. id. A. xiii 45, Otho pellexit (Poppaeam) iuventa ac luxu et quia flagrantissimus in amicitia Neronis habebatur: Dio lxi 11, ἦν δέ τις Μάρκος Σαλούιος ῎Οθων, ὃς οὕτως ἔκ τε τῆς ὁμοιότητος τῶν τρόπων καὶ τῆς κοινωνίας τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων τῷ Νέρωνι ᾠκείωτο ὥστε, κ.τ.λ.: Plut. Galb. 19, φίλῳ δὲ τῷ ῎Οθωνι καὶ συμβιωτῇ διὰ τὴν ἀσωτίαν ἐχρῆτο (ὁ Νέρων). ..

: consuetudo (consuetio, Plaut. Amph. 490) is used in Terence and later writers for intercourse in love (generally illicit love); cf. Calig. 24, 1, cum omnibus sororibus suis stupri consuetudinem fecit: Tit. 10, 2, consuetudinem recordatum, quam cum fratris uxore habuerit: Ner. 35, Octaviae consuetudinem cito aspernatus. The improper relations between Otho and Nero are often referred to; e.g. Aurel. Vict. Caes. 7, Neroni quoque quondam criminose familiaris: Juv. ii 99, pathicus Otho: Mart. vi 32, 2, mollis Otho: Eutrop. vii 17, Otho in privata vita mollis et Neronis familiaris.

: repetundae (sc. pecuniae) denoted the sums of money claimed as a refund from magistrates or officials who had illegally extorted it in Rome or the provinces, and so came to denote the illegal extortion itself. The Lex Calpurnia (149 в.с.) established a perpetua quaestio to try cases of extortion, the penalty being the payment of the amount assessed (litis aestimatio) as illegally taken and the forfeit to the state of the summa sacramenti; the relationship between the Lex Acilia (c. 123 в.с.) and the Lex Servilia (c. 111 в.с.) is obscure, but between them the penalty was raised to double the amount and also included exilium; the Lex Cornelia (of Sulla, 81 B.c.) seems to have made the pecuniary penalty four times the amount and defined the exilium as aquae et ignis interdictio; the Lex Iulia (of Caesar, 59 B.c.) repealed the exilium, retained the litis aestimatio, and ordained that those convicted should lose their rank and be debarred from being senators, judges, witnesses, etc.; cf. Suet. Iul. 43, repetundarum convictos etiam ordine senatorio movit. The Lex Iulia, with some modifications in detail, continued to govern these prosecutions under the empire, the cases being usually tried by the senate. This is the only example of damnatus with the simple abl. of the particular offence, and Ursinus introduced de before repetundis. There is a similar use of the simple abl. in Tac. A. iii 38, Cordum postulaverat repetundis, where Nipperdey inserts de. A general term such as crimine is found with postulare (e.g. Apul. Met. iii 6, vii 3) and Kühner-Stegmann (i 465) cite Cic. Ph. xiii 27, quo scelere damnatus: id. Cael. 78, absolutus ambitu: Sen. Controv. i 5, 1, stupro (al. stupri) accusatur: Suet. Ner. 31, scelere convictos: Sen. Herc. O. 898, scelere (al. sceleris) te misera arguis.

: the tech. term for the restoration of rights which have been forfeited by law: cf. Cic. Agr. ii 4, iudiciorum perturbationes, rerum iudicatarum infirmationes, restitutio damnatorum; so “restituere," e.g. Suet. Iul. 41, Caliy. 15, restituere aliquem (damnatum): Claud. 12, restituere exulem; see also Digest iv 1, 3, “De in integrum restitutionibus.” Tacitus (H. i 77) mentions that Otho as emperor restored to their places in the senate some of those convicted of extortion under Claudius and Nero: redditus Cadio Rufo, Pedio Blaeso, Saevinio Proculo senatorius locus; repetundarum criminibus sub Claudio ac Nerone ceciderant; and it is the restitutio of the senatorius locus which is referred to in our passage.
: see on Vesp. 2, 3.

: cf. Tac. A. i 6, quod postquam Sallustius Crispus particeps secretorum comperit; so “secretorum conscius,' e.g. Suet. Tib. 14, 4. In post-Aug. writers secretum is freely used as a subst. Suetonius has it in the following senses: (a) res secreta "a secret,” here and in Aug. 66, 3, Tib. 14, 4; (b) = secessus “retirement, seclusion," Dom. 3, 1, Tib. 42, 1: 60, Ner. 20, 2, Claud. 10, 1; (c) = locus secretus, Oth. 10, 2 Vesp. 21; (d) = colloquium secretum, Calig. 23, 2, Tib. 25, 3; (e) secreta = litterae secretae “private papers," Calig. 49, 3, in secretis eius reperti sunt duo libelli. ..

: Nero's various efforts to murder his mother Agrippina are described in Ner. 34. Having thrice failed to poison her, he introduced a mechanical device in the ceiling of her bedroom by which the panels would fall on her as she slept, but this design leaked out. He then invited her to Baiae during the festival of the Quinquatrus (March 19-23), and arranged that the vessel on which she came should be run into after her arrival so that it could not be used on her return. In the evening she was entertained to dinner (Suetonius here says by Otho) and when the time came for her to return to Bauli, Nero put her on board a collapsible vessel which would cause her death either by its breaking in pieces or by the falling in of its cabin (solutilis navis, cuius vel naufragio vel camerae ruina periret); she managed, however, to swim ashore. Finally, in the same year 59 A.D., he had her stabbed to death, everything being arranged to make it appear that she had committed suicide in consequence of the failure of a plot of hers to assassinate Nero. See also Tac. 4. xiv 1-9, where the details are given somewhat differently.

: the use of the dative of the gerundive to express end or object, which is comparatively infrequent in pre-class. and class. Lat., is increasingly common from Livy on, especially in Tacitus. For other examples in Suetonius see Dom. 8,2; Vesp. 5, 3:8,5:10; Tit. 8, 4. Kühner-Stegmann (i 746 sqq.) give numerous instances of this dat. with such phrases as comitia edico, indico, habeo; diem dico, indico, statuo; dies venit; tempus do; locum eligo, do, relinquo; finem facio.

: according to Tacitus (A. xiv 4) Agrippina had heard of the plot and in doubt whether she was to believe it she went by litter and not by boat from Bauli to Baiae. There some soothing words from Nero allayed her fears. Dio (lxi 12) says that Nero had brought her with him by sea from Antium to Bauli, using the ship which had been prepared for the murder, in order to accustom her to it.

: in the narrative in Ner. 34 Suetonius does not mention that the banquet was given by Otho, and it is not in Tacitus or Dio; moreover, this account of Otho acting as host to Nero and Agrippina in 59 A.D. contradicts Tacitus (A. xiii 46) who records the sending of Otho to Lusitania among the events of 58, and it is also irreconcilable with what Suetonius says below of the duration of Otho's governorship of Lusitania per decem annos ending in the summer of 68. Furneaux (on Tac. A. xiv 4) suggests that the story about Otho, if true at all, is to be referred to some previous attempt on Agrippina's life.

: Dio (lxi 13), τὴν μητέρα . . φιλοφρόνως εἰστίασεν (ὁ Νέρων): Tac. (l.c.), comiter excepta (Agrippina) superque ipsum (Neronem) collocata. Iam pluribus sermonibus, modo familiaritate iuvenili Nero et rursus adductus ("grave"), quasi seria consociaret, tracto in longum convictu, etc. Comitas was a characteristic of the dinners given by Augustus; cf. Aug. 74, cenam ternis ferculis ("courses'") aut cum abundissime senis praebebat, ut non nimio sumptu, ita summa comitate.

: a daughter of T. Ollius, who perished with Sejanus, but she took the name of her maternal grandfather Poppaeus Sabinus (cons. 9 A.D.). Married first to Rufrius Crispinus, she became the mistress and wife of Otho and mistress and wife of Nero. She induced Nero to murder his mother Agrippina, and to divorce and put to death his wife Octavia. In 63 A.D. she bore to him a son who only lived four months, and when she was again with child in 65 she met her death through Nero kicking her in a fit of rage. Tacitus (A. xiii 45) gives a well-known description of her: Huic mulieri cuncta alia fuere praeter honestum animum. Quippe mater eius, aetatis suae feminas pulchritudine supergressa, gloriam pariter et formam dederat; opes claritudini generis sufficiebant. Sermo comis nec absurdum ingenium: modestiam praeferre et lascivia uti. Rarus in publicum egressus, idque velata parte oris, ne satiaret adspectum, vel quia sic decebat. Famae numquam pepercit, maritos et adulteros non distinguens; neque adfectui suo aut alieno obnoxia, unde utilitas ostenderetur, illuc libidinem transferebat.

: conflicting accounts are given of the exact relationship which existed between Poppaea, Nero, and Otho. In his. earlier work, the Histories (i 13), Tacitus calls her "the imperial mistress," whom Nero had entrusted to Otho until he himself could get rid of his wife Octavia and marry again: Otho pueritiam incuriose, adulescentiam petulanter egerat, gratus Neroni aemulatione luxus. Eoque Poppaeam Sabinam, principale scortum, ut apud conscium libidinum, deposuerat, donec Octaviam uxorem amoliretur. In the Annals (xiii 45-6), however, he says that while her husband Crispinus was still alive she was attracted to Otho by his youth and extravagance and by the fact that he was such an ardent friend of Nero (whom she may have hoped to captivate). This intrigue with Otho was followed at once by their marriage. Nero,. inflamed by Otho's praises of his wife's beauty, sent for Poppaea and fell a complete victim to her charm. She in coquettish fashion pretended that she could not be his, as she was a married woman, and so Nero, to get rid of Otho and have sole possession of her, sent him as governor to Lusitania. (See Fabia, “L'adultère de Néron et de Poppée," Rev. de Phil. 1896 p. 12 sqq., who thinks the account in the Annals is based on more accurate information). Dio (lxi 11) agrees fairly closely with Suetonius and Tacitus in the Histories, saying that Poppaea was taken from her first husband (Crispinus) by Nero and given to Otho and that thus she became the joint mistress of them both (αὐτῇ ἀμφότεροι ἅμα ἐχρῶντο). So too Plutarch (Galb. 19) states that Nero fell in love with her while she was wife to Crispinus, but retaining as yet some respect for his own wife- (Octavia) and fearing his mother (Agrippina) he employed Otho to solicit her. Otho seduced her, promising her that through him she would have Nero as a lover, and persuaded her to leave her husband and marry him. Having married her, he became so jealously fond of her that he would not brook even the emperor as a sharer of her affection, and he was in imminent danger of his life through thwarting Nero's desires; his appointment to Lusitania saved him from death.

: Rufrius Crispinus, a prefect of the praetorians in the reign of Claudius, who was rewarded with “sestertium quindecies et insignia praeturae" for the arrest of Valerius Asiaticus (Tac. A. xi 1 and 4). He was banished by Nero after the conspiracy of Piso in 65, occasione coniurationis, sed Neroni invisus, quod Poppaeam quondam matrimonio tenuerat (A. xv 71). He committed suicide in Sardinia when Nero sent orders for his death (A. xvi 17). demandatam: demandare (= committere, tradere, παρακατατιθέναι) is first found in the title of a play of Caecilius “Demandati''; Livy is the next writer in whom it occurs, e.g. v 27, plures pueri unius curae demandabantur. Suetonius uses it more frequently than any other author; e.g. Ner. 35, 5, privignum mergendum mari. servis ipsius demandavit: Tib. 51, 2, quibus ea funeris sui curam moriens demandarat: Calig. 9, ablegari eum.. et in proximam civitatem demandari (= servandum tradi). ..

: this version of the story makes Nero arrange that Otho was to go through a form of marriage with Poppaea, and was then merely to hold her in trust and inviolate until Nero, freed from Octavia and Agrippina, was ready to take her over.

: poets and post-Aug. prose writers use the infinitive with contentus (= satis habens). In Aug. 82 Suetonius has contentus hoc erat ut. Here, as frequently, corrumpere is used in the sense of διαφθείρειν γυναῖκα.

: Plutarch describes how Otho chafed at the thought of sharing his loved one with any other, and how Poppaea was pleased with this jealous love: ἐλθούσης δὲ παρ᾽ αὐτὸν ὡς γαμετῆς οὐκ ἠγάπα μετέχων, ἀλλ᾽ ἤσγαλλε μεταδιδούς, οὐδὲ αὐτῆς ἀχθομένης, ὥς φασι, τῇ ζηλοτυπίᾳ τῆς Ποππαίας. When emperor, Otho still cherished the memory of Poppaea; cf. Tac. H. i 78, ne tum quidem immemor amorum statuas Poppaeae per senatus consultum reposuit.

div.p: §2. creditur non recepisse: according to Plutarch it was Poppaea who refused to admit Nero when Otho was absent: καὶ γὰρ ἀποκλεῖσαι τὸν Νέρωνα λέγεται μὴ παρόντος τοῦ Ὄθωνος, εἴτε τῆς ἡδονῆς ἀφαιροῦσα τὸ πλήσιμον, εἴτε, ὥς φασιν ἔνιοι, βαρυνομένη τὸν Καίσαρος γάμον, ἐραστῇ δὲ μὴ φεύγουσα χρῆσθαι διὰ τὸ φιλακόλαστον. Plutarch's account agrees with what Tacitus says in his later version (A. xiii 46) of Poppaea discouraging Nero ‘‘nuptam esse se dictitans nec posse matrimonium amittere." See Hardy on Plut. l.c.

p.note: : cf. Tac. H. i 13, Sabinam (apud Othonem) deposuerat (Nero). "depositum” was used of persons as well as things; e.g. in Luc. ii 71 (of Marius hiding in the marshes of Minturnae) stagna avidi texere soli laxaeque paludes | depositum, Fortuna, tuum: Sen. Controv. ii 4, 1, accede huc, puer, depositum, crimen meum: Stat. Ach. i 385 (of the young Achilles entrusted to Lycomedes king of Scyros), depositumque ingens timido commisimus astu.

: so "poscere," Hor. C. i 24, 10, tu frustra pius heu non ita creditum | poscis Quintilium deos. One who denied or refused to return a deposit was called infitiator, e.g. Mart. i 103, 11, In ius, o fallax atque infitiator, eamus; cf. Juv. xiii '60, si depositum non infitietur amicus.

: cf. Sen. Controv. ii 5, 1, nuptias tyrannicidium diduxit, quas non diduxit tyrannus: Hor. C. iii 9, 18, quid si prisca redit Venus diductosque iugo cogit aeneo?: Prop. ii 7, 3, diducere amantes | non queat invitos Iuppiter.
: for this use of seponere see on Tit. 9, 3.

: cf. Tac. H. i 13, mox suspectum (Othonem) in eadem Poppaea in provinciam Lusitaniam specie legationis seposuit. For “per causam” see on Vesp. i. Plutarch (Galb. 20) says that it was Seneca who saved Otho from the jealous Nero by getting him appointed governor: Σενέκαν δὲ εἶχεν εὔνουν, κἀκείνου τὸν Νέρωνα πείσαντος καὶ παραινέσαντος ἐξεπέμφθη Λυσιτανῶν στρατηγός (legatus) ἐπὶ τὸν ᾿Ωκεανόν. Tacitus (A. xiii 46) describes how Otho was cut off from Nero's familiar intercourse, and later excluded from interviews or levées and from the imperial suite, and finally was made governor of Lusitania that he might not be the emperor's rival at Rome: deicitur familiaritate sueta, post congressu et comitatu Otho, et ad postremum, ne in urbe aemulatus ageret, provinciae Lusitaniae praeficitur.

: Lusitania, which earlier was included in Hispania Ulterior, was made into a separate imperial province by Augustus. It comprised nearly all Portugal and a part of Spain (Salamanca and northern Estremadura). The capital was Emerita Augusta (Merida), a colony of veterans founded by Augustus; and Olisipo (Lisbon) and Pax Iulia (Beja) were important towns.
: a correction by Casaubon of et (which is kept by Ihm).
: i.e. death, cf. Plut. Galb. 19, ἐκινδύνευσεν οὖν ὁ Ὄθων ἀποθανεῖν· καὶ παράλογον ἦν, ὅτι τὴν γυναῖκα καὶ ἀδελφὴν ἀποκτείνας διὰ τὸν Ποππαίας γάμον ἐφείσατο τοῦ Ὄθωνος.

: mimus is used occasionally in post-Aug. writers for farcical proceedings or shams of any kind; e.g. Calig. 45 (of Caligula's pretended military triumphs), in hoc quoque mimo praeter modum intemperans: Tib. 24, principatum, quamvis neque occupare confestim neque agere dubitasset, et statione militum, hoc est vi et specie dominationis assumpta, diu tamen recusavit impudentissimo mimo (so Gronovius, animo MSS): Plin. N.H. vii 53, Antiocho regi Syriae e plebe nomine Artemon in tantum similis fuit, ut Laodice coniux regia, necato iam Antiocho, mimum per eum commendationis regnique successionis peregerit: Flor. ii 14, Pseudophilippus regiam formam regium nomen mimo (so Gronov., animo MSS.) quoque regio implevit.

: the subst. distichon (distichum), δίστιχον, was used by Martial, Suetonius, Ausonius, etc. for a couplet of any kind of verse (not merely an elegiac couplet, as Lewis and Short say); e.g. in Suet. Iul. 51 of two trochaic septenarii: Suet. (?) vit. Verg. 58 of two hexameters. The adj. distichos (-us), δίστιχοs, occurs in Varro Men. 398, etiam distichon epigrammation vocant pоета. These lines on Otho seem modelled on Ov. R.A. 161 sq.: Quaeritis Aegisthus quare sit factus adulter? promptu causa est: desidiosus erat. In ..

: Plutarch (Galb. 20) says that Otho quite realised that his governorship was only a specious name and a mere disguise for banishment, and so took care not to make himself disagreeable or oppressive to the provincials: παρέσχεν ἑαυτὸν οὐκ ἄχαριν οὐδὲ ἐπαχθῆ τοῖς ὑπηκόοις, εἰδὼς φυγῆς ὑποκόρισμα καὶ παρακάλυμμα τὴν ἀρχὴν αὐτῷ διδομένην. Cf. Tac. H. i 21 (considerations which influenced Otho in making a bid for empire), praegravem se Neroni fuisse nec Lusitaniam rursus et alterius exilii honorem expectandum. provinciam administravit moderatione: his administration is praised by Tacitus also; H. i 13, comiter administrata provincia; A. xiii 46, provinciae Lusitaniae praeficitur, ubi usque ad civilia arma non ex ("in accordance with'") priore infamia sed integre sancteque egit, procax otii et potestatis temperantior ("a wanton in respect of his hours of idleness, more self-controlled in respect of his official life." Furneaux). quaestorius: Lusitania was an imperial province of the second class, and as such its governor was normally a man of praetorian rank (legatus Augusti propraetore); Otho had held nothing higher than the quaestorship, and was only 26 years of age when appointed. per decem annos: 58-68 A.D. For lengthy tenures of governorships of imperial provinces see on Galb. 9, 1. Nero, of course, had a special reason for keeping Otho away from Rome. abstinentia: opp. to avaritia; see on Tit. 7, 3, abstinuit alieno.

: Tac. H. i 13, primus in partes (Galbae) transgressus nec, donec (“as long as") bellum fuit, segnis et inter praesentes splendidissimus (i.e. most conspicuous of Galba's followers): Plut. Galb. 20, ἀποστάντος δὲ Γάλβα πρῶτος αὐτὸς προσεχώρησε τῶν ἡγεμόνων (“provincial governors''). Plutarch adds that Otho brought with him all his gold and silver vessels to be melted down and coined for Galba's use, and presented him with such of his servants as knew best how to wait upon an emperor; his fidelity and experience were invaluable to Galba, and he accompanied him during all his journey from Spain, driving in the same carriage with him for many days.
: et (= etiam or vel) is omitted in some of the MSS. and of the older editions.

: the name of this astrologer is given as Ptolemaeus by Tacitus and Plutarch. Seleucus was the name of Vespasian's trusty astrologer (Tac. H. ii 78), and Suetonius may have confused the two. Juvenal (vi 557 sqq.) refers to Otho's astrologer without mentioning his name: Praecipuus tamen est horum (sc. astrologorum), qui saepius exul, [ cuius amicitia conducendaque tabella | magnus civis obit et formidatus Othoni, “by whose friendship and by whose venal horoscope a great citizen (i.e. Galba) died, one whom Otho dreaded." Duff. The great influence of the mathematici, or astrologers, in persuading Otho to seize the empire is described in Tac. H. i 22: urgentibus etiam mathematicis, dum novos motus et clarum Othoni annum observatione siderum adfirmant, genus hominum potentibus infidum, sperantibus fallax, quod in civitate nostra et vetabitur semper et retinebitur. Multos secreta Poppaeae mathematicos, pessimum principalis matrimonii instrumentum, habuerant; e quibus Ptolemaeus Othoni in Hispania comes, cum superfuturum eum Neroni promisisset, postquam ex eventu fides, coniectura iam et rumore senium Galbae et iuventam Othonis computantium persuaserat fore ut in imperium ascisceretur. Sed Otho tamquam peritia et monitu fatorum praedicta accipiebat, cupidine ingenii humani libentius obscura credendi. Plutarch (Galb. 23) also mentions the two predictions of Ptolemaeus that Otho would survive Nero and that he would become emperor.
: see on Vitell. 14, 4.
: for the dat. cf. Calig. 7, liberi superstites patri; Suetonius also uses the gen. in Tib. 62, 3, superstes omnium suorum. Cicero and Tacitus have both constructions; see Kühner-Stegmann, i 448 sq.

: Baumg.-Cr. explains this as insuper promittens or novo promisso spondens, a meaning which the word does not seem to bear elsewhere. repromittere was properly a mercantile term for binding oneself to do something in return for a certain consideration; e.g. Plaut. Asin. 453, verum istuc argentum tamen mihi si vis denumerare, | repromittam istoc nomine solutam rem futuram: Cic. Rosc. Com. 13, 37; Suet. Claud. 20, 2, cum quidam privato sumptu emissuros (i.e. that they would drain the Fucine Lake) se repromitterent, si sibi siccati agri concederentur. It was also used merely as a more emphatic form of promittere, e.g. Plin. Εp. iv 27, ad hunc gustum totum librum repromitto (“I guarantee that the whole book is up to the level of this extract'"), and this may be the meaning here and in Tib. 17, 2, eo (cognomine) contentum repromittens quod se defuncto suscepturus esset (i.e. Augustus promised that Tiberius would be satisfied with the title which he would receive on Augustus' death), though there Rolfe translates repromittens ‘‘reiterating the promise," while Bentley and Madvig would read contentum fore promittens; similarly in the present passage Madvig proposed imperatorem promittens. fore

div.p: § 2. nullo genere omisso: Tacitus describes the sedulous efforts of Otho to make himself popular with the army, H. i 23, studia militum iam pridem spe successionis aut paratu facinoris adfectaverat, in itinere (from Spain), in agmine, in stationibus vetustissimum quemque militum nomine vocans ac memoria Neroniani comitatus (their companionship under Nero's régime) contubernales appellando; alios agnoscere, quosdam requirere et pecunia aut gratia iuvare, inserendo saepius querellas et ambiguos de Galba sermones, quaeque alia turbamenta volgi: ib. 36, nec deerat Otho protendens manus adorare volgum, iacere oscula, et omnia serviliter pro dominatione. So Plutarch (Galb. 20) tells how Otho was affable and obliging to everyone (παρέχων ἑαυτὸι· εὐπροσήγορον καὶ φιλάνθρωπον ἅπασιν), and how he specially courted the favour (ἐξεθεράπευσεν) of Vinius (see Suet. Galb. 14, 2) and got preferment for the soldiers from Vinius and the influential freedmen Icelus and Asiaticus.

p.note: : 'attentiveness,” attentions"; cf. Iul. 26,2, nullum officiorum in quemquam genus omisit: ib. 19, 2, omnibus officiis Pompeium assectatus est: Aug. 61, 2, cum praecipua officia vivae praestitisset.

: “favour-seeking,” “popularity-hunting"; cf. Aug. 25, 3, murales coronas quam parcissime et sine ambitione tribuit: Iul. 28, 3, quod per ambitionem data esset (civitas): Tib. 21, 2, ambitione tractus, ut tali successore desiderabilior ipse quandoque fieret.

: cf. Plut. Galb. 20, ὁσάκις δὲ τὸν Γάλβαν εἱστία, τὴν παραφυλάττουσαν ἀεὶ σπεῖραν (“cohort") ἐδέκαζε ("bribed") χρυσοῦν ἑκάστῳ διανέμων, οἷς τιμᾶν αὐτὸν (i.e. Galba) ἐδόκει καταπολιτευόμενος καὶ δημαγωγῶν τὸ στρατιωτικόν. Tacitus (H. i 24) says this bribery was done through the agency of Maevius Pudens, an associate of Tigellinus: Flagrantibus iam militum animis velut faces addiderat Maevius Pudens, e proximis Tigellini. Is mobilissimum quemque ingenio aut pecuniae indigum et in novas cupiditates praecipitem alliciendo eo paulatim progressus est, ut per speciem convivii, quotiens Galba apud Othonem epularetur, cohorti excubias agenti viritim centenos nummos divideret; quam velut publicam largitionem Otho secretioribus apud singulos praemiis intendebat. For quotiens see on Galb. 10, 2.
: see on Galb. 20, 2; an aureus was equivalent to centeni nummi, 100 sesterces, the amount stated by Tac. l.c.

: sc. praetoriae; one praetorian cohort at a time acting as a guard for the emperor at his palace (c. 6, 1) and accompanying him to other houses. The emperors gave to their guards the sportula, or allowance for food, given to clients by patrons (Dom. 7, 1); and Otho, when he was entertaining Galba, took upon himself to play the patron's part towards the guards in attendance on the emperor by bestowing upon them an extravagantly lavish allowance; cf. the words of Tacitus quoted above, “per speciem convivii" (= titulo sportularum).

: Tacitus (H. i 24) gives his name and says that he was one of the imperial bodyguard: adeo animosus corruptor (Otho) ut Cocceio Proculo speculatori de parte finium cum vicino ambigenti universum vicini agrum sua pecunia emptum dono dederit, per socordiam praefecti (i.e. Laco, see on Galb. 14, 2), quem nota pariter et occulta fallebant.

: an “arbiter ex compromisso” to whom the parties agree to leave the decision of the dispute; a magistrate could also refer a case to one arbiter or to more than one, to have it decided in accordance with the principles of bona fides. emancipavit: Torrentius, ingeniously but needlessly, conjectured eique mancipavit. The compound emancipare is used here of the conveyance of land, as in Quintil. vi 3, 44, omnes autem illas (possessiones) Brutus vendiderat; et tum paterna emancipare praedia turpius habebatur: Plin. Ep. x 4, fundos emancipavit et cetera quae in emancipatione implenda solent exigi consummavit, i.e. he went through all the formalities of a fictitious sale (mancipatio per aes et libram) which required the presence of the vendor (qui mancipio dat) and the purchaser (qui mancipio accipit), five witnesses, and a libripens with the scales; the "purchaser" placed a sesterce in the scales held by the libripens and said "hanc ego rem ex iure Quiritium meam esse aio, eaque mihi empta est hoc aere aeneaque libra." See Hardy on Plin. loc. cit. The various senses of emancipare are illustrated in Roby, Rom. Priv. Law, i 75 sqq. ..

: this was also the universal opinion with regard to Galba before he became emperor; cf. the familiar words of Tacitus (H. i 49), maior privato visus, dum privatus fuit, et omnium consensu capax imperii, nisi imperasset.

: Galba's choice of an adopted son and successor is described in Galb. 17, where see notes. Otho's hopes were based on Vinius (Galb. 14, 2), whose daughter Crispina was betrothed to him (Tac. H. i 13, Plut. Galb. 21), and on the support of the soldiers and of Nero's courtiers who recognised in him a kindred nature to Nero, cf. Tac. (l.c.), Otho spem adoptionis statim conceptam acrius in dies rapiebat, faventibus plerisque militum, prona in eum aula Neronis ut similem.

: Plutarch (Galb. 21) says that in preferring him Galba was actuated, as always, by the consideration of what was best for the state: ὁ δὲ Γάλβας ἀεὶ μὲν ἦν δῆλος πρὸ τοῦ ἰδίου τὸ κοινὸν τιθέμενος καὶ ζητῶν οὐχ αὑτῷ θέσθαι (“ to adopt") τὸν ἥδιστον, ἀλλὰ ῾Ῥωμαίοις τὸν ὠφελιμώτατον.

: where decidere is used in earlier writers in this metaphorical sense it takes a preposition; Ter. Heaut. 250, quanta de spe decidi!: Liv. xxxvii 26, Antiochus postquam a spe societatis Prusiae decidit.

: Otho's indignation when he heard the announcement of the adoption of Piso is described in Plut. Galb. 23, τοῦ Ὄθωνος ἐπεφαίνετο πολλὰ σημεῖα τῇ μορφῇ πικρῶς καὶ σὺν ὀργῇ τῆς ἐλπίδος τὴν ἀπότευξιν φέροντος, ἧς πρῶτος ἀξιωθεὶς καὶ τοῦ τυχεῖν ἐγγυτάτω γενόμενος τὸ μὴ τυχεῖν ἐποιεῖτο σημεῖον ἔχθους ἅμα καὶ κακονοίας τοῦ Γάλβα πρὸς αὐτόν: Dio lxiv 5, ἀγανακτήσας ὅτι μὴ αὐτὸς ὑπὸ τοῦ Γάλβα ἐπεποίητο, ἀρχὴν αὖθις μυρίων τοῖς ῾Ρωμαίοις κακῶν παρέσχεν. =

: Plut. c. 21, πεντακισχιλίων μυριάδων ὀφλήμασι βεβαπτισμένος (mersus, obrutus), i.e. 50,000,000 drachmae, 200,000,000 sesterces, about £1,700,000. Tacitus (H. i 21) mentions Otho's ‘luxuria etiam principi onerosa, inopia vix privato toleranda.”
: see on Vesp. 16, 3, professus quadringenties milies opus esse, ut res p. stare posset.

: cadere ab (= interfici ab, cf. ἀποθανεῖν ὑπό, πίπτειν ὑπό) is a poet. constr. very rare in prose: cf. Tac. A. xvi 9, donec a centurione caderet; Sen. Phaedr. 556, a fratre frater, dextera nati parens | cecidit; Ov. Her. ix 36, infesto ne vir ab hoste cadat; xii 18; Met. v 192; Fast. vi 564; Val. Fl. viii 317; (by an oversight in the Thes. Ling. Lat. Livy xxv 19, 5, plures ab Romanis primo incursu equitum ceciderunt, is cited as an ex. of this constr., but there ab Romanis means "on the side of the R.'"). Bentley would alter ab to sub in our passage.

: in the Forum the bankers (mensarii, argentarii) and merchants (negotiatores) transacted their business; there, too, the courts were held and the praetor dealt with the affairs of insolvent debtors. Cf. Foro mersus “bankrupt" (Plaut. Epid. 118), and the common phrase cedere Foro "to become bankrupt." sub creditoribus caderet: the late Lat. constr. cadere sub aliquo, where sub is used in an instrumental sense, was a development of the use of sub to denote attendant circumstances (Kühner-Stegmann, i 571); cf. Flor. iv 4, sub percussore mori. =

div.p: §2. dispensatione: officio dispensatoris; for such trafficking in appointments to imperial stewardships see also Vesp. 23, 2. Instances of т2 the great wealth accumulated by dispensatores are given by Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 p. 70.

p.note: : about £8,500. = decies centena milia sestertium, 1,000,000 sesterces,
: "bodyguard"; see on Galb. 18, 1.

: according to Tac. (H. i 25) there were only two in the first instance, and afterwards a few others were admitted to the plot: Sed tum e libertis Onomastum futuro sceleri praefecit (Otho), a quo Barbium Proculum tesserarium speculatorum et Veturium optionem ("deputy centurion'') eorundem perductos, postquam vario sermone callidos audacesque cognovit, pretio et promissis onerat, data pecunia ad pertemptandos plurium animos. Suscepere duo manipulares ("common soldiers'") imperium populi Romani transferendum et transtulerunt. In conscientiam facinoris pauci adsciti, etc.

: "paid in ready money (praesens pecunia)''; cf. Aug. 101, 2, quam summam repraesentari iussit; Calig. 16, 3; Claud. 18, 1; Ner. 5, 2; 44, 2. Suetonius also uses the word in its wider sense of "doing a thing at once,” lit. “bringing it from the future into the present"; Calig. 58, 1, repraesentare spectaculum voluit; Claud. 34, 1, tormenta quaestionum poenasque parricidarum repraesentabat exigebatque coram; ib. 37, 2, quasi plane repraesentaretur somnii fides (i.e. as if the truth of the dream were being proved at once); Ner. 21, 1, (Nero) repraesentaturum se pollicitus est (i.e. promised that he would sing at once); Vitell. 10, 12, verbera et plagas, saepe vulnera, nonnunquam necem repraesentantes adversantibus.
: sc. sestertia, 50,000 sesterces, about £425.

: "but not so very many"; cf. Aug. 65, 2, C. Lucique casu non adeo fractus: ib. 88, orthographiam non adeo custodit: Galb. 7, 1, valitudo neque adeo gravis. The use of non perinde is similar (see on Galb. 13); so too non (haud, nec, etc.) ita is used in this way very frequently, e.g. Cic. Fam. i 9, 3, non ita magna mercede: Cic. Phil. i 3, 7, nón ita multum provectus. Both Tacitus (H. i 27) and Plutarch (Galb. 25) say that Otho was saluted as emperor at first by only 23 speculatores who carried him off to the camp of the praetorians, their number being increased on the way by other soldiers joining them (see on Oth. 6, 3, obvio quoque adhaerente); they also mention that Otho himself was dismayed by the small number who originally sided with him, and Plut. says that he would have backed out of the venture had he been allowed by the soldiers to do so. Cf. also Dio (Xiph.) lxiv 5, ὑπό τινων στρατιωτῶν ὀλίγων, οἳ συνωμωμόκεσαν αὐτῷ, ἐς τὸ τεῖχος (murum castrorum) ἐσήχθη : Zon. xi 14, ὁ δὲ Ὄθων . . ἐπανέστη αὐτῷ (i.e. Galba) τριάκοντα μόνους στρατιώτας ἑτοιμασάμενος. ..

: Gruter aptly quotes Tac. A. iv 7, primas dominandi spes in arduo: ubi sis ingressus, adesse studia et ministros; cf. also Tac. H. i 55, insita mortalibus natura propere sequi quae piget inchoare. The acc. c. inf. depending on fiducia occurs earlier in Ov. A.A. i 269, prima tuae menti veniat fiducia cunctas | posse capi: ib. ii 349: Liv. xxxvi 7: Sen. Ep. 32, 2, habeo quidem fiduciam non posse te detorqueri: Tac. A. xi 28, ipsa facilitas imperatoris fiduciam dabat posse opprimi damnatam ante quam ream. Suetonius uses the same constr. with fides, persuasio, suspicio, rumor, opinio, spes, metus, mos, religio, etc. ..

: the expression animus fert (only here in Suet.) is mainly poetical, though found a few times in Sall. and Liv.; cf. Ov. Her. xiii 85, volui revocare animusque ferebat: Hor. E. i 14, 8: Sall. Cat. 58, 6, diutius in his locis esse, si maxime animus ferat, frumenti .. egestas prohiberet: Sall. Iug. 54, 4: Liv. xxiii 15, xxx 12, xl 4. It is used with the inf., as here, in Ov. Met. i 1, In nova fert animus mutatas dicere formas | corpora: Luc. i 67: Pers. iv 7. Some of our MSS. have erat for tulerat, and Ursinus read fuerat (cf. Iul. 82, 4, fuerat animus coniuratis corpus occisi in Tiberim trahere).

: Piso was adopted by Galba on Jan. 10, 69 A.D., and on Jan. 15 Galba was slain and Otho was proclaimed emperor by the soldiers. The design which Suetonius here attributes to Otho of attacking Galba immediately after the adoption is not mentioned elsewhere; Tacitus (H. i 26) says that the conspirators had thoughts of carrying off Otho to the camp on the evening of Jan. 14, but refrained: adeoque parata apud malos seditio, etiam apud integros dissimulata fuit, ut postero iduum die redeuntem a cena Othonem rapturi fuerint, ni incerta noctis et tota urbe sparsa militum castra nec facilem inter temulentos consensum timuissent.
: i.e. the castra praetoria; see on Galb. 19, 1.

: used here for the period of duty during which one out of the twelve praetorian cohorts acted as guard at the imperial palace. Other meanings of statio in Suet. are: (1) posts where soldiers are stationed as guards; e.g. Iul. 32, cum plurimi etiam ex stationibus milites concucurrissent: (2) the soldiers stationed as guards; e.g. Aug. 32, 1, dispositis per opportuna loca stationibus: (3) more especially the soldiers stationed as guards at the palace, e.g. Tib. 24, 1, statione militum, hoc est vi et specie dominationis, assumpta: Ner. 21, 1, adiuvante vulgi preces etiam

: the two conspirators who took the leading part in the assassination of Gaius Caligula were Cassius Chaerea and Cornelius Sabinus, who were both tribunes of a cohort of the praetorian guard. The two prefects of the praetorian guard had been accused of complicity in an earlier conspiracy against that emperor (Calig. 56 and 58).

: Nero tried to induce the tribunes and centurions of the praetorian guard to accompany him in a last despairing flight from Rome, but they either openly refused or gave evasive answers; one even exclaimed in the words of Virgil "Usque adeone mori miserum est?” Waking at midnight, he found that his guard had left (comperit stationem recessisse), and he fled from the city with only four faithful attendants (Ner. 47).
: between Jan. 10 and Jan. 15; see on Galb. 17, intra sextum adoptionis diem.

: portents, evil omens; cf. Ner. 19, 1, turbatus religione simul ac periculo ("by a threatening portent'"): Tib. 2, 2, per contemptum religionis (''in defiance of the portent'"): Oth. 8, 3. It is not necessary to assume a reference to “dies religiosi” (Claud. 14, Tib. 61, 2), i.e. days in the Roman year which were unfavourable for any undertaking, generally because they were dedicated to the worship of the gods of the underworld or were associated with some historical disaster to the Roman people and so were dies atri or vitiosi, e.g. the day of the battle of the Allia, July 18 (Vitell. 11, 2); other dies religiosi were the dies postriduani (Vitell. '8, 1, n.). See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii² 295.
: the astrologer; see c. 4, 1.

: eximere diem, tempus, etc., meant to take away a day, etc., from a purpose for which it might have been used, and so to waste it; cf. Liv. i 50, 8, quia ea res exemisset illum diem: Cic. Q. Fr. ii 4, Lentulus dies comitiales exemit omnes: Cic. Phil. vi 3, 7, horam eximere ullam in tali cive liberando sine scelere non possumus: Sen. N. Q. iii 1, damna aetatis male exemptae labor sarciat. To "talk out" a bill in the senate was “diem dicendo eximere” (Cic. Att. iv 3, Q. Fr. ii 1).

div.p: § 2. sub aede Saturni: this temple of Saturn was dedicated in 497 B.c. (Liv. ii 21, Dion. Hal. vi 1); it was situated “sub clivo Capitolino” (Serv. on Aen. ii 115, viii 319: Varr. L.L. v 42: Fest. p. 322 Müll.: Dion. Hal. i 34, παρὰ τῇ ῥίζῃ τοῦ λόφου κατὰ τὴν ἄνοδον τὴν ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς (Fori) φέρουσαν εἰς τὸ Καπιτώλιον). Munatius Plancus restored it under Augustus (Suet. Aug. 29). See Jordan, Topogr. Rom i 2, 360 sqq.

p.note: : cf. Tac. H. i 27, Otho .. ad miliarium aureum sub aedem Saturni pergit. This miliarium or milepost of bronze gilt was erected at the upper end of the Forum by Augustus as curator viarum in 20 B.C.; cf. Dio liv 8, προστάτης τῶν περὶ τὴν ῾Ρώμην ὁδῶν αἱρεθεὶς τὸ χρυσοῦν μίλιον κεκλημένον ἔστησε. Plutarch (Galb. 24) describes it as the centre at which all the roads of Italy terminated; the mileposts, however, on these roads marked the distances, not from the miliarium aureum, but from the gates of the city. Pliny (N.H. iii 66) mentions it as the starting-point in the survey of Rome under Vespasian: mensura currente a miliario in capite Romani Fori statuto.
: at the emperor's morning reception or levée (salutatio); see on Vesp. 4, 4.

: cf. Tib. 10, 2, paucos .. in digressu exosculatus: Ner. 37, 3, neque adveniens neque proficiscens quemquam osculo impertiit, ac ne resalutatione quidem. The amici principis of the first order, and senators as the emperor's peers received the honour of the imperial kiss; cf. Plin. Pan. 23 (on Trajan's entry into Rome as emperor), gratum erat cunctis, quod senatum osculo exciperes, ut dimissus osculo fueras; Pliny also praises Trajan for not requiring his fellow-citizens to kiss his feet and for not returning their kiss with his hand: ib. 24, non tu civium amplexus ad pedes tuos deprimis nec osculum manu reddis. Caligula, according to Dio lix 27 (cf. Sen. Ben. ii 12), kissed very few; to most, even to senators, he gave his hand or foot to kiss. Nero showed his animosity against the senate by refusing to kiss them when he set out for Greece and on his return from his tour (Ner. 37, 3, quoted above). Agricola on his return from Britain visited Domitian and was greeted with a hasty kiss, but the emperor held no converse with him (Tac. Agr. 40, exceptus brevi osculo et nullo sermone). The custom of the imperial kiss, which was probably introduced from the East, is discussed at length by Friedlaender, Sitteng. i10 95 sq.; see also Marquardt, Privatl.2 260.

: this use of interesse c. dat. pers. (= adesse) is very remarkable; the normal expression would be sacrificio eius interfuit; there does not seem to be any parallel passage (Freund, De Suet. genere dicendi, cites Sen. Prov. i 1, cum probaremus interesse nobis Deum, which is quite different). Ernesti conjectured superfuit, for which see on Tit. 1. This sacrifice and the soothsayer's warnings of the danger threatening Galba are mentioned in Galb. 19, 1. Otho was the only senator present at the sacrifice; cf. Dio lxiv 5, οὕτως ὑπ' αὐτοῦ (i.e. Galba) ἐτιμᾶτο ὥστε καὶ ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ, ἐν ᾗ ἀπέθανε, θυομένῳ αὐτῷ μόνος τῶν βουλευτῶν παρέστη.

: this freedman was Onomastus; Tac. H. і 27, nec multo post libertus Onomastus nuntiat exspectari eum ab architecto et redemptoribus (“contractors'"); quae significatio coeuntium iam militum et paratae coniurationis convenerat. •

: Tac. (l.c.), Otho causam digressus requirentibus cum emi sibi praedia (“country-house") vetustate suspecta eoque prius exploranda finxisset, innixus liberto per Tiberianam domum in Velabrum, inde ad miliarium aureum pergit. So too Plutarch (Galb. 24) says that Otho's pretext was that he had bought an old house and wanted to point out to the vendors any defects (τὰ ὕποπτα δεῖξαι τοῖς πωληταῖς). Under Roman law such defects had to be pointed out before the contract was actually made, for after that time the thing bought was at the buyer's risk (Hardy on Plut. l.c.).

: = per Tiberianam domum (Tac.); διὰ τῆς Τιβερίου καλουμένης οἰκίας (Plut.). The domus Tiberiana (see Vitell. 15, 3) near the N.W. corner of the Palatine hill was at the back of the palace of Augustus (domus Augustana) and connected with it. It looked down on the Velabrum. From the Velabrum Otho entered the Forum through the vicus Tuscus.

: the appointed place of meeting, viz. the miliarium aureum in the Forum. "constitutum'' is often used as a subst. for an appointed time and place of meeting, a tryst: e.g. Varr. R.R. ii 5, 1, qui tum sero venisset ad constitutum: Cic. Caecin. 33, qui ad constitutum experiundi iuris gratia venissent: Cic. Att. xii 1, 1, v Kalend, igitur ad constitutum ("on the 26th, then, to our tryst'').

: this feigned illness is implied in the account of Tacitus (H. i 27), who says that Otho leant on a freedman (innixus liberto) when leaving the palace (cf. id. Ann. ii 29, Libo aegritudine fessus seu simulato morbo innisus fratri). Suetonius, on the other hand, says that Otho rushed (proripuit se) from the Palace.

div.p: §3. abditus: "hidden away in" the closed sedan; cf. Vitell. 16, abstrusus gestatoria sella. For the abl. with abdere see on Vitell. 7, 2.

p.note: : this was probably a cathedra, a sedan-chair fashioned like the cathedra or chair ordinarily used by women (Marquardt, Privatl.” 726, 737), and differing in shape from the usual sedan-chair (sella gestatoria, for which see Vitell. 16, and Dom. 2, 1, where it is distinguished from the lectica). The cathedra is mentioned in Juv. i 65, cum iam sexta cervice feratur | hinc atque inde patens ac nuda paene cathedra. These sedanchairs were roofed over and the openings at the side could be shut close with curtains; cf. Juv. i 124, ostendens vacuam et clausam pro coniuge sellam: Mart. xi 98, 11, lectica nec te tuta pelle veloque, | nec vindicabit sella saepius clausa. Modest women had the sedan-chair closed; cf. Sen. de Remed. 16, 7: Ben. i 9.
: lecticarii (φορειαφόροι Plut.) was the general term for bearers of either the lectica or sella. Sidonius (Ep. i 11, 9) has cathedrarii for the bearers of the cathedra.
: the calcei were fastened with leather straps (corrigiae, lora); see Marquardt, op. cit. 590: Daremberg-Saglio, i 816.

: "taken up on their shoulders.” succollare is first used in Varr. R.R. iii 16, 8, of bees carrying the king-bee: apes fessum (regem) sublevant, et si nequit volare, succollant (in Verg. G. iv 217 this is expressed by regem attollunt umeris). It was the regular word for the lecticarii taking on their shoulders the poles (asseres) of the lectica; e.g. Suet. Claud. 10, 2, ab his (militibus) lecticae impositus est et, quia sui diffugerant, vicissim succollantibus in castra delatus est (cf. Catull. 10, 21, fractum qui veteris pedem grabati | in collo sibi collocare posset). The account given here by Suetonius differs in details from that in Plutarch and Tacitus. According to Plut., Galb. 25, when Otho reached the miliarium aureum in the Forum, he was saluted as emperor by 23 soldiers. Frightened at the fewness of his supporters he began to waver, but these soldiers would not let him recede; they drew their swords and surrounding his litter ordered the bearers to proceed, while Otho kept ejaculating that he was ruined and urged the bearers to make haste. Tacitus (H. i 27) says: Ibi tres et viginti speculatores consalutatum imperatorem ac paucitate salutantium trepidum et sellae festinanter impositum strictis mucronibus rapiunt.
: cf. Galb. 10, 1.

: see on Oth. 1, 2. Plutarch (l.c.) describes how on Otho's arrival at the camp the tribune on duty, Martialis, in the confusion of the moment opened the gate, and then there was no more opposition, for those who were ignorant of the plot, finding themselves in the midst of its supporters, at once came over; so too Tac. (c. 28): stationem in castris agebat Iulius Martialis tribunus; is magnitudine subiti sceleris, an corrupta latius castra, et, si contra tenderet, exitium metuens, praebuit plerisque suspicionem conscientiae. Anteposuere ceteri quoque tribuni centurionesque praesentia dubiis et honestis, isque habitus animorum fuit, ut pessimum facinus auderent pauci, plures vellent, omnes paterentur.

: Plutarch says that while Otho was being borne through the Forum, his 23 original supporters were increased by 23 more, and that on the way from the Forum to the camp others kept joining by threes and fours at a time. Tacitus merely states that the original 23 were joined by about the same number on the way to the camp: totidem fere milites in itinere adgregantur, alii conscientia, plerique miraculo ("curiosity"), pars clamore et caudiis, pars silentio, animum ex eventu sumpturi. 1 1 :

: for the slaughter of Galba by the "equites, quibus mandata caedes erat" see Galb. 19, 2. Piso, after temporarily effecting an escape to the temple of Vesta, was dragged out and slain by Otho's emissaries: Tac. H. i 43, advenere missu Othonis nominatim in caedem eius ardentes Sulpicius Florus e Britannicis cohortibus, nuper a Galba civitate donatus, et Statius Murcus speculator, a quibus protractus Piso in foribus templi trucidatur.
: see on Vesp. 7, 3 for this use of pro. Tacitus (c. 36) says that Otho delivered his speech to the soldiers "pro vallo castrorum.”

: there is nothing corresponding to these words in the elaborate speech which Tacitus (cc. 37, 38) puts into the mouth of Otho, a speech consisting of a denunciation of the cruelty and meanness of Galba, and an appeal to the soldiers to champion the rights of the people and the senate. Dio (lxiv 5), like Suetonius, attributes to Otho no long discourse; he simply says that Otho persuaded or rather bought the soldiers (προσαναπείσας, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐκπριάμενος). Macé, op. cit. p. 206, suggests that Suetonius here is indirectly criticizing Tacitus: “En racontant vivement ces événements rapides, Suétone, qui n'embellit point la réalité, ne fait prononcer à Othon qu'une phrase fort courte: 'J'aurai ce que vous me laissez!' dit-il aux soldats. Et le biographe ajoute: 'Il ne leur fit point de plus longue harangue, ni plus de promesses, ni plus de protestations. Cette allusion ne serait-elle point une critique discrètement adressée par le modeste biographe à l'éloquent historien?" There can be little doubt that Fabia (Sources de Tacite p. 140) is right in saying "Tacite a fabriqué le beau discours d'Othon de toutes pièces.” =

: solum, tantum, a post-Aug. use of the word; cf. Aug. 16, 3, uno demum navigio aegerrime effugit: Val. Max. viii 14, 6, id enim demum ornamenti familiae consulatibus et sacerdotiis et triumphis celeberrimae deerat: Quintil. xi 3, 68, adeo suis demum oculis credidit: i 4, 29, quaedam verba tertiae demum personae figura dicuntur, ut licet, piget: Traian. ad Plin. Εp. x 22, nobis autem utilitas demum spectanda est. See also on Vitell. 14, 5.
: in post-Aug. writers vergere is used of time; e.g. Тас. А. іі 43, nam suam aetatem vergere ("was declining''), Drusi nondum satis adolevisse: xi 4, vergente autumno: xii 44, vergentibus iam annis
: xiii 38, vergente iam die: Curt. iv 7, 9, nox vergit ad lucem. This is the only place where Suetonius uses the verb.

: the meeting of the servile senate to heap honours on Otho, while the bodies of the dead still lay in the Forum, is mentioned in Tac. H. i 47 as the crowning horror of that awful day: Exacto per scelera die novissimum malorum fuit laetitia. Vocat senatum praetor urbanus; certant adulationibus ceteri magistratus. Adcurrunt patres; decernitur Othoni tribunicia potestas et nomen Augusti et omnes principum honores, adnitentibus cunctis abotere convicia et probra, quae promisce iacta haesisse animo eius nemo sensit: omisisset offensas an distulisset, brevitate imperii in incerto fuit. Cf. Plut. Galb. 28, Εὐθὺς δὲ βουλὴ συνεκαλεῖτο. Καὶ καθάπερ ἄλλοι γεγονότες ἢ θεῶν ἄλλων γεγονότων συνελθόντες ὤμνυον ὅρκον ὑπὲρ τοῦ Οθωνος, ὃν αὐτὸς ὀμόσας οὐκ ἐτήρησε, κ.τ.λ. The senate was convened by the praeter urbanus, as both consuls, Galba and Vinius, were dead.

: ratione is a correction by Erasmus of oratione. Elsewhere ponere rationem is used in the literal sense of making a reckoning or furnishing an account; e.g. Digest xlvi 3, 89, ratione posita eius pecuniae: xlvii 4, 1, ponere rationem actus quem servus administravit : Sen. Ep. 87, cum ad patrimonium ventum est, diligentissimi computatores sic rationem ponitis singulorum quibus aut pecuniam credituri estis aut beneficia (= rationem initis facultatum eorum quibus "you make calculations concerning'"). This reading is accepted by Roth and Preud 'homme, but not by Ihm. Oudendorp preferred propositaque ratione. Ernesti tried to defend ponere orationem as equivalent to habere orationem. Burman proposed expositoque brevi oratione, explaining exposito as an abl. abs. like cognito, intellecto, perspecto, etc., while the clause with quasi gives the gist of the speech. Similarly Walther suggested positoque oratione, citing Cic. Orat. 4, positum sit in primis sine philosophia non posse effici eloquentem: id. Cael. 7, posuistis enim coniurationis hunc participem fuisse: id. Verr. ii 38, tantum verbo posuit. There is not, however, any instance in Suet. of such a use of the abl. abs. Bentley wildly conjectured perfunctusque or professusque brevi oratione. Erasmus' correction is strongly supported by Spart. Sev. 7, where Septimius Severus tries to justify to the senate his seizing the imperial power: in curia reddidit rationem suscepti imperii causatusque est, quod ad se occidendum Iulianus notos ducum caedibus misisset. ..

: Otho's defence, that he had acted under compulsion of the soldiers and that he had endangered his life by trying to oppose their wishes, is mentioned in Dio lxiv 8, βεβιάσθαι μὲν γάρ, καὶ ἐς τὸ τεῖχος (murum castrorum) ἄκων ἐσῆχθαι, κἀνταῦθα ἀντιλέγων κεκινδυνευκέναι ἔλεγε.

: Mommsen (Staatsr. ii³ 791 n. 6) notices that from the practice of the soldiers hurrying away the newly acclaimed emperor in a lectica or sella to the camp (Suet. Claud. 10, Ner. 8; Tac. A. xii 69, H. і 27) the verb rapi came to be used by metonymy for the elevation to the throne; e.g. Capitolin. Max. et Balb. 3, qui statim raptus est et novo genere senatus consulti, cum eodem die senatus consultum factum esset, inductus in curiam Caesar est appellatus.

: Tac. H. i 47, Otho cruento adhuc foro per stragem iacentium in Capitolium atque inde in Palatium vectus. For the Palatium or domus Palatina see on Vesp. 25. petit is perf. (= petiit), as in Vitell. 2,5; 16; Vesp. 24; Tit. 10, 1. Ihm and Preud'homme read petit in 18 passages, petiit only once (Calig. 14, 3). =
: praeter; see on Vesp. 24.

: cf. Plut. Oth. 3, τοῖς δὲ πολλοῖς χαριζόμενος οὐκ ἔφευγε τὸ πρῶτον ἐν τοῖς θεάτροις Νέρων προσαγορεύεσθαι: Dio lxiv 8, τὸ γοῦν ὄνομα αὐτοῦ (i.e. Nero) αὑτῷ εὐθὺς ἐπέθετο: Tac. H. i 78, Creditus est etiam de celebranda Neronis memoria agitavisse spe volgum alliciendi. Et fuere qui imagines Neronis proponerent; atque etiam Othoni quibusdam diebus populus et miles, tanquam nobilitatem et decus adstruerent, Neroni Othoni acclamavit (greeted him with shouts of "Nero Otho"). Ipse in suspenso tenuit (i.e. he left it undecided whether he would accept the title) vetandi metu vel agnoscendi pudore. The populace in their first exultation at Nero 's death put on caps of freedom (Ner. 57, 1, tantum gaudium publice praebuit ut plebs pilleata tota urbe discurreret), but they soon longed for a revival of his lavish expenditure on food and spectacles provided for their entertainment.

: a favourite form of expression with Suetonius; cf. Claud. 43, signa quaedam nec obscura paenitentis dederat: Calig. 12, 2, suspicionem retinentis dabat: Ner. 40, 4, ut gaudentis etiam suspicionem praeberet: Iul. 2, non sine rumore prostratae pudicitiae.

: Plutarch (Oth. 3) cites Cluvius Rufus as authority for the statement that the name of Nero was added to that of Otho on the imperial passports sent to Spain for use in the postal service: Κλούβιος δὲ ῾Ροῦφος εἰς ᾿Ιβηρίαν φησὶ κομισθῆναι διπλώματα, οἷς ἐκπέμπουσι τοὺς γραμματηφόρους, τὸ τοῦ Νέρωνος θετὸν ὄνομα προσγεγραμμένον ἔχοντα τῷ τοῦ ῎Οθωνος. Plutarch adds that Otho discontinued this when he observed the irritation it caused to the aristocracy. The historian Cluvius Rufus was already an ex-consul at the time of Caligula's death (41 A.D.); he accompanied Nero on his musical tour in Greece (Ner. 21); Galba appointed him as his successor in the governorship of Hispania Tarraconensis (Tac. H. і 8), and he retained this post under Vitellius (H. ii '65). He is described as “perinde dives et eloquentia clarus'” (H. iv 43). As a historian he wrote on the reigns of Nero, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius (cf. Tac. A. xiii 20, xiv 2). See also Introd. c. iii.

: a diploma (δίπλωμα) consisted of two folding tablets; such tablets were used to convey official authorisations and answered to our permits and passports. They were issued to couriers carrying public despatches, and also to those who were given the privilege of using the State means of conveyance, the cursus publicus established by Augustus. They were granted by the emperor or a provincial governor, and the holder was entitled to have his journey expedited in every way by the provision of fresh horses, etc.; cf. Tac. H. ii 54 where the diplomata Othonis are mentioned as ensuring rapid travelling. Such diplomata were inscribed with the name of the reigning emperor, the name of the authorised person, and the period for which they were available: they became invalid on the emperor's death. For a full description and illustrations of these and of military diplomata (conferring such rights as civitas and connubium on time-expired soldiers) see the articles by Thédenat in Daremberg-Saglio ii 266 sqq., and by Purser in Smith's Dict. Ant. i3 641 sqq.; cf. also Marquardt Staatsv. i² 561.
: see on Vesp. 6, 4.

: cf. Plut. Oth. 3, καί τινων εἰκόνας Νέρωνος εἰς τοὐμφανὲς προθεμένων οὐκ ἐκώλυσε: Tac. H. i 78, et fuere qui imagines Neronis proponerent. The statues of hated emperors were overthrown after their death; cf. Dom. 23, 1, and the instances given by Friedlaender, Sitteng. iii¹º 59.

: we are not told who these were or when they were deprived of their positions by Galba. In Galb. 20, 2 Patrobius, a freedman of Nero, is mentioned as having been executed by Galba. Dio (lxiv 8) says that Otho was intimate with Nero's infamous freedman Sporus, and that he frightened the people by making use of the other favourites of that emperor. Tacitus (H. i 76) states that Crescens, a freedman of Nero, ingratiated himself with Otho by giving a banquet to the people of Africa in honour of Otho's accession. Most of the notorious freedmen of Nero, such as Polyclitus, Doryphorus, and Helius, were already dead, but Epaphroditus, Nero's a libellis (“receiver of petitions''), was also a libellis to Domitian (see Dom. 14, 4); it is not known whether he was reappointed under Otho and continued in office down to Domitian's reign.

: Otho signed the order authorising the (procurator) a rationibus, or chief controller of the fiscus, to pay the amount. The fiscus was the emperor's own treasury; see on Vesp. 16, 3. The cost of building palaces was defrayed from it (Stat. Silv. iii 3, 103; Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 950, 1003). The emperor's signature to official documents is mentioned also in Ner. 10, 2, cum de supplicio cuiusdam capite damnati, ut ex more subscriberet, admoneretur: Calig. 29, 2, numerum puniendorum subscribens.
: quingenties centena milia sestertium, 50,000,000 sesterces, about £425,000. =

: for the first of his two palaces, the Domus Transitoria or House of Passage (so called as connecting the Palatine with the Esquiline), Nero took the whole of the Palatine, the Velia, the valley of the Colosseum, the S.-E. portion of the Esquiline, including the gardens of Maecenas, and up to the Servian agger. This palace was destroyed in the great fire of 64 A.D., and he then began the even more wildly extravagant Aurea Domus with a vestibule big enough to contain his colossal statue, 120 ft. high (see on Vesp. 18), and with a triple colonnade a mile long. All the parts of the palace were overlaid with gold and adorned with gems and mother-of-pearl. He dedicated it, though not finished, and said that he was at last beginning to be housed like a human being (Ner. 31, 2, hactenus comprobavit, ut se diceret quasi hominem tandem habitare coepisse). Though Otho continued the building during his brief reign, it was never completed. Vespasian stopped the work and restored the ground to the public, confining the limits of the imperial residence to the Palatine itself. ..

div.p: § 2. dicitur obmurmurasse: the construction of this sentence is twofold: first dicitur is used personally with the nom. and inf. (pave factus edidisse), but later we have the acc. and inf. (prolapsum obmurmurasse) depending on dicitur in an impersonal sense. In c. 12 infr. there is the same variation with traditur followed by fuisse scambus and later by linere consuetum. Similar mixed constructions are found in Cic., Liv., etc.; e.g. Cic. de or. ii 299, ad Themistoclem quidam doctus homo accessisse dicitur eique artem memoriae pollicitus esse se traditurum; cum ille quaesisset, quidnam illa ars efficere posset, dixisse illum doctorem, ut omnia meminisset, etc.; Liv. v 41, M. Papirius dicitur Gallo barbam suam permulcenti scipione eburno in caput incusso iram movisse; atque ab eo initium caedis ortum, ceteros in sedibus suis trucidatos. See KühnerStegmann, i 710.

p.note: : = per somnum; cf. Vesp. 7,2; 25.

: cf. the troubled dreams of Caligula, Calig. 50, 3, neque enim plus quam tribus nocturnis horis quiescebat ac ne iis quidem placida quiete, sed pavida miris rerum imaginibus.
