Nero's sleep was broken by frightful visions after he had murdered his mother Agrippina and his wife Octavia (Ner. 46). repertus humi: Dio lxiv 7, καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο τῆς νυκτὸς οὕτω δή τι ἐν τοῖς ὕπνοις ἐταράχθη, ὥστε καὶ ἐκ τῆς εὐνῆς ἐκπεσεῖν, τοὺς δὲ προκοιτοῦντας (ante cubiculum excubantes) ἐκπλῆξαι. ἐσπηδήσαντες οὖν εὗρον αὐτὸν χαμαὶ κείμενον.

: the Manes of one whose death was due to outrage did not rest till the guilty paid the penalty or made fitting atonement; cf. Liv. iii 58, manes Verginiae per tot domos ad petendas poenas vagati nullo relicto sonte tandem quieverunt. When the survivor of the three Horatii, after vanquishing the three Curiatii, slew his sister Horatia for bewailing their death, though he was acquitted by the people as having slain her justly, yet his father had to offer expiatory sacrifices (“piacularia sacrificia") for the bloodshed, and these sacrifices were continued every year by the Horatian family to the Manes of Horatia (Liv. i 26, Тас. А. xii 8). Agrippina invokes against Nero the shades of the Silani whom he had murdered (Tac. A. xiii 14, infernos Silanorum manes invocare). There is a remarkable story in Apul. Met. viii 9 sqq. of the vengeance exacted by a wife, in obedience to the Manes of her murdered husband, from a would-be lover of hers who had been his murderer.
: Dio (l.c.) says that it was after his unsuccessful sacrifice on the first day.

: a most unlucky omen; cf. Iul. 59, cum immolanti aufugisset hostia, profectionem adversus Scipionem et Iubam non distulit. Prolapsus (πεσὼν ἐπὶ στόμα, Dio xlii 58) etiam in egressu navis verso ad melius omine: “Teneo te,” inquit, ‘“Africa.” The Crassi, father and son, both fell at the doors of the temple of Astarte at Hierapolis in Syria, an omen of the disaster they were to meet with at Carrhae (Plut. Crass. 17).

: in the few other passages where this compound is found it means to murmur or mutter against; e.g. Ov. Her. xviii 47 (Leander complaining of Boreas), Vana peto; precibusque meis obmurmurat ipse: Frontin. Strat. iv 6, 2 (of the mutterings of soldiers against their general), cum unus ex eis obmurmurando diceret. In our passage the ob- seems to have little force, though it may be intensive as in obverberare, etc. Roby (Lat. Gram. ii p. 415) gives a list of compound verbs in which ob- is "almost pleonastic.” Τί γάρ μοι καὶ μακροῖς αὐλοῖς;: SC. κοινόν ἐστι, ‘“What have I to do with long pipes?” Dio (lxiv 7) gives the words in a slightly different form: θύοντί τε γὰρ αὐτῷ τὴν θυσίαν τὴν πρώτην τὰ ἱερὰ πονηρὰ ὤφθη, ὥστ᾽ αὐτὸν μεταγνόντα ἐπὶ τοῖς πεπραγμένοις εἰπεῖν “τί γάρ με ἔδει μακροῖς αὐλοῖς αὐλεῖν;” ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο δημῶδες, ἐς παροιμίαν φέρον, ἐπὶ τῶν ἔξω τι τοῦ προσφόρου σφισι ποιούντων. The expression which Dio thus describes as proverbially used of unfitting and unprofitable effort is not found elsewhere; the meaning as applied to Otho would be that given by Torrentius, "Non omnibus buccis longas tibias, quae difficilius inflentur quo longiores sint, pariter convenire, ut neque Othoni imperium.” Burman cites as parallel the lines of Soph. (frag. 701, Nauck) which Cicero (Att. ii 16) applies to Pompey: φυσᾷ γὰρ οὐ σμικροῖσιν αὐλίσκοις ἔτι, | ἀλλ' ἀγρίαις φύσαισι, φορβειᾶς ἄτερ ‘“He blows no more upon a tiny pipe, But with a fierce unmodulated blast." Were it not for the statement of Dio, it would be easy with some of the early commentators to take Otho's words as meaning "What use is there in my trying to sacrifice or to make atonement?'"; long pipes being used especially in connexion with sacrifices (see Daremberg-Saglio, v 304). Cedrenus (11 cent.) differs from other authors in stating (p. 216 C) that the words were the dying words of Otho: θύων δέ ποτε ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ τὰ τῆς ᾿Αφροδίτης ᾄσματα τοῖς ἱεροῖς παρέμιξε· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο, Οὐιτελίου (Vitellius) αὐτῷ ἐπαναστάντος, ξιφιδίῳ ἑαυτὸν διεχρήσατο, εἰπών “ Τί γάρ με ἔδει μακροῖς αὐλοῖς ἄδειν καὶ αὐλεῖν;”

: on January 1, 69 A.D., the oath of fealty to Galba was taken by the army of Lower Germany; but in Upper Germany the 4th and 22nd legions took the oath to the senate and people of Rome. News of this was brought to Vitellius at Cologne and he communicated it to the officers of the army of Lower Germany of which he was legatus. On January 3 Vitellius was proclaimed emperor by the troops of both armies (Vitell. 8, Tac. H. i 52 sqq.). Galba was deliberating about the adoption of a son and successor when the revolt occurred; cf. Plut. Galb. 22, καταλαμβάνει δ' αὐτὸν ἔτι μέλλοντα καὶ βουλευόμενον ἐκραγέντα τὰ Γερμανικά. When the tidings reached him, he proceeded at once to adopt Piso on January 10 (Suet. Galb. 17, Oth. 5, 1; Plut. Galb. 23). On January 15 Galba and Piso were slain, and Otho was made emperor.
: for this adj. see on Vesp. 6, 2. The legions composing the armies in Upper and Lower Germany are mentioned in the notes on Galb. 16, 2 and Vitell. 8, 1.
: the usual expression for swearing allegiance; see on Galb. 11.

: Vitellius was appointed by Galba to the command in Lower Germany (Vitell. 7, Tac. H. i 9). He arrived there about December 1, 68 A.D.; so that he had been just a month in command when both armies declared him emperor.
: see on Vesp. 11, auctor senatui fuit decernendi.

: Galba had already sent envoys to the mutinous German armies on the occasion of his adoption of Piso, but these envoys were recalled by Otho who sent others to replace them; cf. Tac. H. i 74, Otho, revocatis quos Galba miserat legatis, rursus ad utrumque Germanicum exercitum et ad legionem Italicam easque, quae Lugduni agebant, copias specie senatus (“nominally from the senate'') misit. Legati apud Vitellium remansere promptius quam ut retenti viderentur; praetoriani, quos per simulationem officii legatis Otho adiunxerat, remissi, antequam legionibus miscerentur.

: Tac. (l.c.), Crebrae interim et muliebribus blandimentis infectae ab Othone ad Vitellium epistulae offerebant pecuniam et gratiam et quemcumque quietis locum prodigae vitae legisset. Plutarch (Oth. 4) says that when Otho's confidence was restored by the receipt of friendly despatches from Mucianus and Vespasian, who were in command of large forces in Syria and Judaea, he wrote to Vitellius advising him to remember his position as a soldier (παραινῶν στρατιωτικὰ φρονεῖν) and offering him large sums of money and a city where he could live in luxurious ease. Vitellius at first replied in a hypocritical strain, but soon both he and Otho grew heated and wrote in most abusive terms, charging each other with disgraceful vices of which they were both equally guilty according to Plutarch and Tacitus.

: Otho's offer to share the empire with Vitellius is mentioned also in Dio lxiv 10: ὁ δὲ Ὄθων, ἐπειδὴ καὶ μὴ ἔπειθε τὸν Οὐιτέλλιον, ἐς κοινωνίαν αὐτὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς πολλάκις παρακαλῶν, εἰς πόλεμον λοιπὸν φανερὸν καθίστατο. For the position of the consors imperii in relation to the princeps see on Tit. 9, 3.

: Suetonius alone states that Otho proposed to become the son-in-law of Vitellius. The daughter of Vitellius is mentioned in Vitell. 6; for her marriage to D. Valerius Asiaticus and her subsequent marriage in Vespasian's reign see on Vesp. 14, 1.

: Vitellius, having been proclaimed emperor by the armies in Germany, was joined by various commanders in Gaul and by the troops in Britain. He sent Fabius Valens and Aulus Caecina in advance with two forces to invade Italy by different routes; see Vitell. 9 and the notes there.
: Tacitus (H. i 80) says that this outbreak of the praetorians nearly brought about the destruction of the whole city: Parvo initio, unde nihil timebatur, orta seditio prope urbi excidio fuit.
: = senatorii ordinis; see on Vesp. 2, 3.

div.p: § 2. placuerat per classiarios arma transferri remittique navibus: a most obscure passage, and it is possible that some words have been lost, since in all the better MSS. et is found before placuerat, though it has been generally deleted by editors as being due merely to the preceding est. Lipsius suggested etenim for et, Oudendorp Ostiam, Bücheler ei. The military riot which Suetonius mentions is described by Tacitus (H. i 80) and Plutarch (Oth. 3), but it is very difficult to reconcile the three accounts. The account given by Tac. is as follows:-Septumam decumam cohortem e colonia Ostiensi in urbem acciri Otho iusserat; armandae eius cura Vario Crispino tribuno e praetorianis data. Is quo magis vacuus quietis castris iussa exequeretur, vehicula cohortis incipiente nocte onerari aperto armamentario iubet. Tempus in suspicionem, causa in crimen, adfectatio quietis in tumultum evaluit, et visa inter temulentos arma cupidinem sui movere. Fremit miles et tribunos centurionesque 'proditionis arguit, tamquam familiae senatorum ad perniciem Othonis armarentur, pars ignari et vino graves, pessimus quisque in occasionem praedarum, volgus, ut mos est, cuiuscumque motus novi cupidum; et obsequia meliorum nox abstulerat. Resistentem seditioni tribunum et severissimos centurionum obtruncant, rapta arma, nudati gladii, insidentes equis urbem ac Palatium petunt. Plutarch says: Κρισπῖνον δὲ πέμψαντος αὐτοῦ τὴν ἑπτακαιδεκάτην σπεῖραν Ωστίας ἀπάξοντα, κἀκείνου νυκτός ἔτι συσκευαζομένου καὶ τὰ ὅπλα ταῖς ἁμάξαις ἐπιτιθέντος, οἱ θρασύτατοι πάντες ἐβόων οὐδὲν ὑγιὲς τὸν Κρισπῖνον ἥκειν διανοούμενον, ἀλλὰ τὴν σύγκλητον (senatum) ἐπιχειρεῖν πράγμασι νεωτέροις καὶ τὰ ὅπλα κατὰ Καίσαρος, οὐ Καίσαρι παρακομίζεσθαι. Τοῦ δὲ λόγου πολλῶν ἁπτομένου καὶ παροξύνοντος οἱ μὲν ἐπελαμβάνοντο τῶν ἁμαξῶν, οἱ δὲ τοὺς ἐνισταμένους ἑκατοντάρχας δύο καὶ τὸν Κρισπῖνον αὐτὸν ἀπέκτειναν, πάντες δὲ διασκευασάμενοι καὶ παρακαλέσαντες ἀλλήλους Καίσαρι βοηθεῖν ἤλαυνον εἰς τὴν ῾Ῥώμην. From Plutarch's account it appears that Crispinus had been sent to Ostia to bring the 17th cohort to Rome; that the disturbance began in the camp at Ostia; and that the rioters rode from Ostia to Rome. It is not clear whether Tac. means that the mutiny began at Ostia, and that the mutineers on their arrival at Rome were joined by the praetorians, or that the outbreak occurred in the praetorian camp outside the gates of Rome, from which the praetorians rode into the city to the Palace. Most probably Tac. is in agreement with Suet. that the mutiny took place in the praetorian camp, and that the mutineers were praetorians. Hardy (on Plut. l.c.) understands Tac. to mean that the 17th cohort had already arrived in the city, having been brought from Ostia to be converted into a praetorian cohort, and that while Crispinus was taking the arms for its equipment out of the armoury in the praetorian camp, the praetorians, suspecting some treachery, mutinied. Hardy accepts Mommsen's view that this 17th cohort, stationed at Ostia, was one of the cohortes urbanae, while others hold that it was one of the cohortes civium Romanorum or that it consisted of marines (classiarii); see note on Vesp. 8, 3. The account given by Suet. here of the cause of the disorder is so condensed as to be almost unintelligible. The best explanation of his words is that given by Krauss (De vitarum imperatoris Othonis fide quaestiones, p. 27): “Ut septima decima cohors classiariorum Ostiae collocata iustis ad bellum armis instrueretur, classiarii cum vehiculis in castra praetoriana, ubi armamentarium publicum erat, praemissi et inde arma vehiculis imposita ad Tiberim transportare impositaque navibus Ostiam transferre iussi erant. Vocabulum "Remittere" significare videtur, armamentarium praetorianorum omnibus cohortibus circa Romam tendentibus commune fuisse illamque cohortem, ut in pace, arma sua habuisse in illo deposita et reservata, unde bello exorto cohortibus singulis reddebantur.” Hofstee infers from Tac. H. ii 63 that the 17th cohort returned to Ostia from Rome during Otho's reign, and thinks that Suet. is describing the trouble as happening in the praetorian camp at the time when the arms were being taken out to be sent back to Ostia on the cohort's return. Both Tac. and Plut., however, definitely connect the disorder with the bringing of the cohort from Ostia to Rome, and not with its return. remitti: Stephanus suggested praemitti, which is approved of by Burman and Ernesti; Oudendorp (followed by Wolf and Bremi) demitti (= secundo flumine devehi Ostiam).

p.note: : the praetorian camp; for its origin and situation see on Galb. 19, 1.

: i.e. given out of the armoury (armamentarium) in the praetorian camp which served also as a depot for the cohorts in the neighbourhood of Rome and contained arms for every class of troops (cf. Tac. H. i 38). By an oversight Howard and Jackson in their Index verborum to Suetonius take promerentur here from promereor.

: where Otho was entertaining at dinner eighty of the senators with their wives; Plut. (l.c.), πυθόμενοι παρ' αὐτῷ δειπνεῖν ὀγδοήκοντα συγκλητικοὺς ἐφέροντο πρὸς τὰ βασίλεια: Tac. (c. 81), erat Othoni celebre convivium primoribus feminis virisque.

: Plutarch says that the rioters rode from Ostia to Rome (ἤλαυνον εἰς τὴν Ρώμην), a distance of 16 miles, but if the 17th cohort at Ostia was one of the cohortes urbanae (Mommsen, Hermes xvi 645), the difficulty is that there were no cavalry attached to the cohortes urbanae (Mommsen, Staatsr. ii³ 1067); if the trouble began in the praetorian camp, then the words of Tacitus “insidentes equis urbem ac Palatium petunt” are to be explained by the fact that the praetorian camp lay outside the city of Rome, and there was a squadron of 24 cavalry attached to each praetorian cohort (Heraeus on Tac. l.c.; Marquardt, Staatsv. ii² 477).

: Tac. (c. 82), undique arma et minae, modo in centuriones tribunosque, modo in senatum universum, lymphatis caeco pavore animis, et quia neminem unum destinare irae poterant, licentiam in omnes poscentibus: Plut. (l.c.), νῦν καιρὸν εἶναι λέγοντες ἐν ταὐτῷ πάντας ἀνελεῖν τοὺς Καίσαρος πολεμίους.

: Tac. (l.c.), volnerato Iulio Martiale tribuno et Vitellio Saturnino praefecto legionis, dum ruentibus obsistunt. Both Tac. and Plut. say that Otho sent out the prefects of the praetorians to try to appease the soldiers, while the senatorial guests made their escape from the Palace by another door.
: neither Tac. nor Plut. mentions any officers slain at the Palace, though some had been slain earlier at the praetorian camp.

: ut, sic ut (sicut), erat, etc., like the Gr. ὡς εἶχεν, denote the state or condition in which a person or thing was when an action took place (Kühner-Stegmann, ii 451); cf. Calig. 45, 2, sic ut erant loricatos ad discumbendum adhortatus est: Claud. 9, 1, sic ut vestitus advenerat : Claud. 34, 2, induxit unum (in arenam), sic ut erat togatus.

: Tac. (l.c.), militum impetus ne foribus quidem Palatii coercitus, quo minus convivium inrumperent, ostendi sibi Othonem expostulantes. Plut. says that they forced their way in, asking what had become of the enemies of Caesar (i.e. the senators).

: Otho stood up on a couch and succeeded in quieting them with entreaties and tears; cf. Tac. (l.c), donec Otho contra decus imperii toro insistens precibus et lacrimis aegre cohibuit, redieruntque in castra inviti neque innocentes: Plut. (l.c.) ὀρθὸς ἀπὸ τῆς κλίνης πολλὰ παρηγορήσας καὶ δεηθεὶς καὶ μηδὲ δακρύων φεισάμενος μόλις ἀπέπεμψεν αὐτούς. Οn the following day the prefects harangued them and paid 5000 sesterces to each man. Then Otho ventured to enter the camp and was surrounded by the tribunes and centurions wishing to resign command of such mutinous troops. The soldiers were shamed by this and returned to their duty, even demanding the punishment of the ringleaders, two of whom were executed.

div.p: § 3. praepropere: Tacitus (c. 89) mentions two reasons for his haste: aspernatus est omnem cunctationem ut Neroni quoque exitiosam; et Caecina iam Alpes transgressus extimulabat. Bentley's praepostere is needless.

p.note: : owing to the express testimony of the grammarian Diomedes (Keil, i 365) that Suetonius in one of his writings defended the form incohare against inchoare, Ihm restores incohare everywhere in the Lives of the Caesars, though the MSS. give inchoare, which is retained by Preud'homme.
: see on c. 6, 1. The

: cf. Tac. (l.c.), fuere qui proficiscenti Othoni moras religionemque nondum conditorum ancilium afferrent. The ancilia, or sacred shields, were 12 in number, 11 being copies of the original shield which fell from heaven on March 1 in the reign of Numa. name ancile is for ancidile (am-caedere "to cut on both sides''), the shield being an oval with incisions at both sides, so that it roughly resembled the figure 8. On March 1, the opening of the campaigning season, the ancilia were brought out (moveri, cf. κινεῖν τὰ ὅπλα) from the sacrarium Martis (or curia Saliorum in Palatio) by the Salii, or priests of Mars, who in a warlike dance (tripudium; hence their name Salii, a saliendo) and with special chants (axamenta) bore them round various halting-places (mansiones) where the ancilia were deposited for one night while the Salii feasted, and not until the end of March were the ancilia put back (condi) into the sacrarium Martis. There was a minor festival (Armilustrium) on Oct. 19 (the campaigning season, in theory, ending in Oct.), when the ancilia were again brought out and put back.

: it was inauspicious to make a march “ancilibus nondum conditis,” as we see from Liv. xxxvii 33 where Scipio is retarded by this consideration: stativa deinde ad Hellespontum aliquamdiu habuerunt, quia dies forte, quibus ancilia moventur, religiosi ad iter inciderant (for dies religiosi see on “religio,” Oth. 6, 1). It was also an inauspicious time for marriage; cf. Ov. Fast. iii 393, Nubere si qua voles, quamvis properabitis ambo, | differ; habent parvae commoda magna morae. | Arma movent pugnam, pugna est aliena maritis. | Condita cum fuerint, aptius omen erit. .....

: Otho set out on March 24 according to Suetonius, but on March 14 according to Tacitus (H. i 90). The date given by Tac. is apparently confirmed by the Acta Fratr. Arval. for 69 A.D. (Henzen p. xciii = Dessau Inscr. Lat. 241): pri(die) idus Martias vota nuncupata pro s[al]ute et reditu... (Vitelli has been erased) Germanici imp(eratoris). In his note on this Dessau says: “Pridie idus Martias, quo die Othonem ab urbe profectum esse narrat Tac. H. i 90, pro huius sine dubio salute et reditu vota nuncupata sunt ab Arvalibus; sed devicto Othone, cum nondum acta huius diei perscripta essent, pro Othonis nomine, Vitellii positum; id ipsum postea erasum. De nomine Germanico Vitellio indito cf. Tac. H. i 62, ii 64.'"

: in 205 B.c., during the second Punic war, the worship of the Magna Mater (Cybele) was introduced to Rome from Pessinus in Galatia, and the festival of the Megalesia (Μεγάλη = Magna) was held annually from April 4 to April 10. Under the emperor Claudius (41-54 A.D.) another religious celebration was instituted to commemorate the grief of Cybele at the loss of Attis, and her joy when he was restored. This celebration was held from March 22 to March 27. The first day, March 22, was the day of Arbor intrat, when the priests (Dendrophoroi) carried a pine-tree, on which hung an image of Attis, to the temple of Cybele on the Palatine. On March 23 there was a sounding of trumpets (περισαλπισμός, tubilustrium). March 24 (the day on which Suet. says Otho set out) was the day of blood (dies sanguinis) on which the chief priest (Archigallus) gashed his arm and sprinkled the blood. March 25 was a day of rejoicing (Hilaria) for the restoration of the body of Attis to Cybele. March 26 was a day of rest (requietio), and on March 27 the celebration concluded with the lavatio or bathing of the image of the goddess in the Almo where it joins the Tiber. See Marquardt, Staatsv. iii 367 sqq.; R. Ellis, Introd. to Catull. lxiii.

: in addition to the unfavourable auspices which Suetonius mentions here, most alarming prodigies were reported; cf. Tac. H. i 86, Prodigia insuper terrebant diversis auctoribus volgata: in vestibulo Capitolii omissas habenas bigae, cui Victoria institerat; erupisse cella Iunonis maiorem humana speciem; statuam divi Iulii in insula Tiberini amnis sereno et immoto die ab Occidente in Orientem conversam; prolocutum in Etruria bovem, insolitos animalium partus et plura alia rudibus saeculis etiam in pace observata, quae nunc tantum in metu audiuntur. The omission of these prodigies by the superstitious Suetonius is one of the proofs that he did not follow Tacitus as his authority.

: Dis pater was the Italian equivalent of the Greek Pluto, god of the underworld. The name is traditionally explained as di(ve)s "rich” (cf. Πλούτων from πλοῦτος “riches''), but some philologists derive it from the stem div (in divus, divinus, Dialis, etc.). Dis pater was a son of Saturn and Ops, and brother of Jupiter and Neptune. His oldest shrine at Rome was connected with the temple of Saturn at the foot of the Capitol. The worship of Dis first comes into prominence at Rome in 249 B.C., while the issue of the first Punic war was uncertain; alarming portents occurred, such as the destruction of part of the walls of Rome by lightning, and the Sibylline books ordained that ludi Tarentini were to be celebrated in honour of Dis and Proserpina in the Campus Martius for three successive nights, and that black victims (hostiae furvae) were to be offered, and that these ceremonies were to be renewed every hundred years (see on the “ludi saeculares,” Dom. 4, 3). Except in this connexion we hear little of the worship of Dis at Rome either in the state religion or in private cults. For the offering of black cattle to the gods of the underworld, as of white victims to the di superi, cf. Verg. Aen. vi 153, 243 sqq.; Serv. on Verg. G. ii 380. ..

: litare (καλλιερεῖν) is probably used here of the victim itself (= felicem esse); cf. Aug. 96, 2, sacrificio non litanti: Mart. x 73, 6, non quacumque manu victima caesa litat. Suetonius also has litare in the more usual sense of the sacrificer obtaining favourable omens: Iul. 81, 4, pluribus hostiis caesis, cum litare non posset: Ner. 56, attendit et extispicio, nec unquam litavit.

: this peculiarity of the litatio in the case of sacrifices to Dis is not mentioned elsewhere, and seems a mere generalisation from the fate of Otho. Bouché-Leclercq (in Daremberg-Saglio iii 1268), commenting on this statement of Suetonius, says: “Cette casuistique suspecte est contraire à l'essence même du sacrifice expiatoire ou propitiatoire, qui est la substitution de la victime à la personne menacée, laquelle se rachète par cette rançon acceptée. A. ce compte, les nombreux sacrifices offerts aux divinités souterraines, durant les Jeux Séculaires (Tellus, Dis Pater, Proserpine, les Moeres) auraient dû, pour être heureux, présenter des entrailles défavorables, ce qui est absurde.”

: described more fully in Tac. H. i 86, Sed praecipuus et cum praesenti exitio etiam futuri pavor subita inundatione Tiberis, qui immenso auctu, proruto ponte sublicio (i.e. the old wooden U 2 bridge) ac strage obstantis molis refusus, non modo iacentia et plana urbis loca, sed secura eiusmodi casuum implevit. Rapti e publico plerique, plures in tabernis et cubilibus intercepti. Fames in volgus inopia quaestus et penuria alimentorum. Corrupta stagnantibus aquis insularum ("tenement houses”) fundamenta, dein remeante flumine dilapsa. Plutarch (Oth. 4) says that the river rose to an unprecedented height: Καὶ τὸ περὶ τὸν Θύμβριν σύμπτωμα σημεῖον ἐποιοῦντο οἱ πολλοὶ μοχθηρόν. Ἦν μὲν γὰρ ὥρα περὶ ἦν μάλιστα οἱ ποταμοὶ πλήθουσιν, ἀλλ᾽ οὔπω τοσοῦτος ἤρθη πρότερον οὐδὲ ἀπώλεσε τοσαῦτα καὶ διέφθειρεν ὑπερχυθεὶς καὶ κατακλύσας πολὺ μέρος τῆς πόλεως, πλεῖστον δὲ ἐν ᾧ τὸν ἐπὶ πράσει διαπωλοῦσι σῖτον (i. e. the corn-market), ὡς δεινὴν ἀπορίαν ἡμερῶν συχνῶν κατασχεῖν. Pliny (N.H. iii 55) says that the inundations of the Tiber were prophetic of impending dangers: quin immo vates intelligitur potius ac monitor, auctu semper religiosus verius quam saevus. We hear of disastrous inundations in B.c. 241, 215, 202, 193-2, 189, 54, 44 (cf. Hor. C. i 2), 27, 23, 22. Augustus tried to protect Rome by appointing “Curatores alvei (“bed”) Tibéris et riparum,” but the inundations still continued, and in 15 A.D. we find the senate considering (and rejecting) a scheme to lessen the volume of the river by diverting some of its main tributaries, the Nar, Velinus, and Clanis (Dio lvii 14, Tac. A. i 76).

: the 20th milestone on the Via Flaminia which ran up the valley of the Tiber through Etruria and continued through Umbria and over the Apennines to Ariminum (Rimini) on the Adriatic. A station "Ad Vicesimum" on the Via Flaminia is mentioned in the Jerusalem Itinerary and the Peutinger Table; Bunbury (Smith's Dict. Geogr. ii 1300) says that it must have been a little beyond the Monte di Guardia, but was evidently a mere Mutatio, or station for changing horses, and no ruins mark the site.

: cf. Tас. Н. і 86, utque primum vacuus a periculo animus fuit, id ipsum, quod paranti expeditionem Othoni campus Martius et via Flaminia iter belli esset obstructum, a (“without regard to'") fortuitis vel naturalibus causis in prodigium et omen imminentium cladium vertebatur.

: cf. Tac. H. ii 30, Otho consultavit, trahi bellum an fortunam experiri placeret. When the armies of Valens and Caecina, the generals of Vitellius, had effected a junction, the combined force in their fortified camp outside Cremona was nearly 100,000 men, and they were ready to give battle. At the council of Otho's commanders, which Otho himself attended, Suetonius Paulinus and Marius Celsus were strongly in favour of delay, Otho was inclined to risk a decisive battle (pronus ad certandum), and his brother Titianus along with Proculus, prefect of the praetorian guard, with the rashness of ignorance (imperitia properantes) advocated this course, which was adopted with disastrous results.
: see on Vesp. 16, 3. Kraffert would read quoad.

: one of the arguments for delay used by Suetonius Paulinus, the most skilful of Otho's officers (nemo illa tempestate militaris rei callidior habebatur, Tac. c. 32). He urged that the full forces of Vitellius had already come: that no troops from Britain or Spain could reach him: that Gaul was ready to rise, and that Vitellius could withdraw no more men from the Rhine: that Gallia Narbonensis had been cowed by Otho's fleet and by his land forces: that Italy beyond the Padus was shut in by the Alps and could not be relieved by sea and was already exhausted by the passage of the Vitellian forces who now lacked corn and supplies: that Otho had behind him all the resources of the state and vast reserves of money "stronger than the sword in civil war"; and by delaying he would allow of the arrival of reinforcements from Pannonia, Moesia, Dalmatia, and the East.

: this is the view of Tacitus (c. 40), who describes how Titianus and Proculus had recourse to their rights as commanders-in-chief (in ius imperii transeunt) to overrule Paulinus and Celsus, and ordered the attack which was angrily demanded in a despatch from Otho: Aderat citus equo Numida cum atrocibus mandatis, quibus Otho increpita ducum segnitia, rem in discrimen mitti iubebat, aeger mora et spei impatiens. So too Plutarch (Oth. 9) says on the authority of Secundus, Otho's secretary, that Otho was no longer able to endure the suspense; his inexperience and effeminacy made him incapable of a rational consideration of the dangers; overburdened by his cares, he hurried on, and, with head veiled, like a man who leaps from a precipice, he committed the fortunes of his party to the accidents of chance: δοκεῖ δὲ μηδὲ αὐτὸς Ὄθων ἐξαναφέρειν ἔτι πρὸς τὴν ἀδηλότητα μηδὲ ὑπομένειν ἀηθείᾳ καὶ μαλακότητι τοὺς περὶ τῶν δεινῶν λογισμούς, ἐκπονούμενος δὲ ταῖς φροντίσι σπεύδειν ἐγκαλυψάμενος, ὥσπερ ἀπὸ κρημνοῦ, μεθεῖναι τὰ πράγματα πρὸς τὸ συντυχόν. Both Plut. and Tac. mention another account that the two armies, considering neither Otho nor Vitellius worth fighting for, were inclined to come to terms and either give the empire to one of their own generals (Paulinus having the best chance, according to Tac.) or leave the choice to the senate. Plut. adds that some suspect that this design was one reason why Celsus and Paulinus advised delay, while the adherents of Otho (Proculus and Titianus) wished for immediate action. Tac. (c. 37) rejects this version as improbable.

: Vitellius had just set out from Lower Germany bringing up the remaining strength of the army of Germany and 8000 men levied in Britain, when news reached him of his victory at Betriacum and the death of Otho. See Tac., c. 57.

: "that victory could be gained to a very large extent." The expression is peculiar, as profligari must be taken impersonally, plurimum being adverbial (cf. Galb. 5, 2; 8, 1; Dom. 4, 2; so "plus,” Galb. 15, 1). In all the other passages where Suetonius uses profligare, it means "to conquer": Iul. 30, 4, Pharsalica acie caesos profligatosque adversarios prospiciens; ib. 35, 2, Mithridatis filium una acie profligavit; Ner. 3, 1, nec nisi partibus ubique profligatis M. Antonio. tradidit classem. Gellius (xv 5) says that profligare means “ad perniciem deducere,” “deperdere,” and that it was often wrongly used in the sense of "prope absolvi" "to be almost completed” (Cicero, however, uses it in this latter sense, Tusc. v 6, 15, profligata iam haec et paene ad exitum adducta quaestio est, and the phrase profligare bellum, “to break the back of the war," occurs in Cic., Liv., Tac., etc.). In our passage profligari is usually explained as prope absolvi, but the use of plurimum seems = fatal to this; it would be a meaningless pleonasm to say "the matter could be almost decided to a very large extent." For the impersonal use of the passive see on Vitell. 1, 1, variatum esset.

: Plutarch includes in the reasons for Otho's decision for immediate action the indisputable fact that the praetorian cohorts, now coming to taste what real campaigning was, longed to return to the luxurious life of Rome, and therefore could not be restrained in their eagerness for a battle, for they imagined that they would sweep the enemy at the first charge (οὐκ ἦσαν καθεκτοὶ σπεύδοντες ἐπὶ τὴν μάχην, ὡς εὐθὺς ἐξ ἐπιδρομῆς ἀναρπασόμενοι τοὺς ἐναντίους). substitit Brixelli: Brixellum (mod. Brescello) was a town of Cisalpine Gaul on the south side of the Padus (Po). When the council of Otho and his commanders decided on a battle, Titianus and Proculus prevailed on Otho to retire to Brixellum, while Paulinus and Celsus did not oppose this for fear of being thought to expose the emperor to peril. This mistake gave the death-blow to the party of Otho; cf. Tac. H. ii 33, Is primus dies Othonianas partes afflixit; namque et cum ipso praetorianarum cohortium et speculatorum (see on Galb. 18, 1) equitumque valida manus discessit, et remanentium fractus animus, quando suspecti duces et Otho, cui uni apud militem fides, dum et ipse non nisi militibus credit, imperia ducum in incerto reliquerat. Similarly Plutarch (Oth. 10) characterizes Otho's withdrawal as a blunder, not merely because it removed the respect and emulation which his presence would have inspired, but also because he took away with him the keenest and most efficient of the troops as his bodyguard (ὡσπερεὶ στόμωμα τῆς δυνάμεως ἀπέκοψε). Dio (lxiv 10) says that Otho withdrew from the battle, declaring that he could not bear to witness a battle between kindred; just as if he himself had become emperor in any legal fashion and not by butchering the consuls and the Caesar (i.e. Piso) and the emperor (Galba) in Rome itself.

div.p: § 2. apud Alpes: this victory seems to have been a very paltry affair. Some of Otho's troops were sent up to seize the province of the Maritime Alps and then attack Gallia Narbonensis which had declared for Vitellius. The province of the Maritime Alps was on the borders of Italy and Narbonensis. Augustus had made it a separate province under a procurator. Tacitus (ii 12) describes how Otho's troops on their march devastated Italy like a foreign land, and how Marius Maturus, the procurator of the Maritime Alps, hastily raised a levy of the natives to resist the invasion of his province; but these raw forces were speedily routed by Otho's trained soldiers, who took vengeance by burning Albintimilium (Ventimiglia). In Gallia Narbonensis the troops of Otho, supported by his fleet, twice defeated the detachments sent by Fabius Valens for the protection of the province; but they withdrew after their victories to Albigaunum (Albenga) in Liguria.

p.note: : mod. Piacenza, on the south bank of the Padus, near where that river is joined by the Trebia. It was defended by Othonian troops under Vestricius Spurinna, and Caecina, crossing the Padus, assaulted it unsuccessfully and had to retreat across the river to his camp at Cremona. A corps of gladiators who fought for Otho made their way over to the northern bank and routed the Vitellian auxiliaries near Cremona. When Otho's generals (Paulinus, Celsus, and Gallus) would not follow up this success, they were accused of treason by their own men, and Otho summoned his brother Titianus, who was prefect at Rome, to act as generalissimo of his army (Tac. ii 17-23).

: sc. aedes, the place being named from the temple of Castor and Pollux there; Tacitus (ii 24) calls it “locus Castorum,” Orosius (vii 8, 6) more briefly "Castores” (Pliny, N.H. vii 86, x 121, similarly calls the temple of the twins Castor and Pollux at Rome, “aedes Castorum''). Lucien Herr (Revue de Philol. xvii, 1893, p. 208 sqq.) argues that locus castorum (not Castorum) should be read in Tac. (l.c.), the meaning being "the place of beavers (fibrorum)” which were numerous in the rivers of that region. He thinks that Suetonius misunderstood “castorum” and wrote "ad Castoris" as if the god were referred to. Tacitus defines the position of the place as 12 miles E. of Cremona on the Via Postumia in the direction of Betriacum and Mantua. The Othonian forces under Paulinus, Celsus, and Gallus were now concentrated at Betriacum. Caecina with the Vitellians at Cremona, eager to wipe out his defeat at Placentia, arranged an ambush on the Via Postumia to ensnare the Othonians at Locus Castorum, but Celsus and Paulinus skilfully planted a counter-ambuscade and encircled the forces of Caecina; Paulinus, however, for some mysterious reason (treachery was freely hinted at) did not press his advantage, though it seems that he might have utterly routed the Vitellians and captured their camp at Cremona. See Tac. ii 24-26, Plut. Oth. 7, and the excellent description (with plan) of the battle of Locus Castorum in Bury's Student's Roman Empire c. 19.

: the name of this village appears with different spellings: the best MSS. of Suetonius give the form with "t" (corruptly here bretiacum, in Vitell. 10 betriacensi, in Vesp. 5 bretiacensi); Βητριακόν occurs in Plut. Oth. 8; Betricum in Eutrop. vii 17; Tacitus (H. ii 42, etc.) uses Bedriacum, so too Pliny (N.H. x 135) Bedriacensibus bellis; in Juvenal ii 106 the MSS. give Bebriacis campis, and the adj. Bebriacus is found in the Schol. on that line and also on line 99, as well as in Priscian ii 43. Lucien Herr (see preceding note) thinks the true form is Bebriacum, a Celtic name from the same root bebr or bibr as appears in Bebronna, Bibrax, Bibracte, Bibroci, etc., so that the meaning of Bebriacum is “pagus fibrorum” i.e. "district of beavers," and “locus castorum” in Tac. H. ii 24 is a translation of it. See Friedlaender on Juv. ii 106, and Hofstee on our passage. Tacitus (ii 23) describes the position of

: inter Veronam Cremonamque situs est vicus, duabus iam Romanis cladibus notus infaustusque (i.e. the defeat of Otho's forces on Apr. 14 (?), 69 A.D. by Caecina and Valens, and the defeat of Caecina and Valens towards the end of Oct. in the same year by Antonius Primus the lieutenant of Vespasian). Neither of the two battles of Betriacum was fought at Betriacum itself, but on the road from it to Cremona and much nearer to Cremona, the attacking forces advancing from Betriacum. The battle which proved so disastrous to Otho was fought partly on the high road and partly in the groves and vineyards at either side; cf. Tac. ii 42, Et per locos arboribus ac vineis impeditos non una pugnae facies: comminus eminus, catervis et cuneis concurrebant. In aggere viae (i.e. the raised causeway of the Via Postumia) conlato gradu corporibus et umbonibus niti, omisso pilorum iactu gladiis et securibus galeas loricasque perrumpere: noscentes inter se, ceteris conspicui, in eventum totius belli certabant. The army of Otho broke and fled to Betriacum and capitulated on the following morning. For a discussion of Otho's strategy see Henderson, Civil War and Rebellion in the Rom. Emp. 92 sqq., and the criticism of Henderson's views by Hardy, J. Ph. xxxi 123 sqq.

: cf. Tac. ii 41, where we are told that two of Otho's officers came asking for a parley with Caecina, and before he could reply scouts reported that Otho's forces were already advancing to attack: Eodem die ad Caecinam operi pontis intentum duo praetorianarum cohortium tribuni conloquium eius postulantes venerunt. Audire condiciones ac reddere parabat, cum praecipites exploratores adesse hostem nuntiavere. Interruptus tribunorum sermo, eoque incertum fuit, insidias an proditionem vel aliquod honestum consilium coeptaverint. Tacitus goes on to tell how when Otho's army came near to the enemy a sudden rumour spread among them that the army (Plut., Oth. 12, says the generals) of Vitellius had deserted. Whether this rumour was spread by the spies of Vitellius or originated through treachery or by chance among the partizans of Otho, was never known. The Othonians took the initiative in peaceful overtures by greeting the foe (ultro salutavere), but were answered by angry shouts, while several on their own side, hearing and not understanding the greeting, thought they were being betrayed. Any further misunderstanding was prevented by the Vitellians making a fierce onslaught. Plutarch gives the same account and says that the van of Otho's army greeted their adversaries in friendly fashion as fellow-soldiers (ἠσπάσαντο φιλίως συστρατιώτας προσαγορεύσαντες).

: this is the reading of Q.; the other MSS., including M, have consultatione (‘“'nescio an rectius" Ihm). consalutatio is used in the same way of soldiers' mutual greetings in Tac. H. iv 72, nulla inter coeuntes exercitus consalutatio; id. A. xv 16, maesti manipuli prae fletu usurpata consalutatio. , vix

div.p: § 3. impetum capit: "came to a quick decision," "formed a sudden resolve (subitum consilium)" on the analogy of capere consilium; cf. Calig. 43, expeditionis Germanicae impetum cepit: Aug. 42, 3, impetum se cepisse scribit frumentationes abolendi: Ner. 48, 1, revocato rursus impetu "changing his hasty resolve”: Curt. v 12, 1, Bessus occidendi protinus regis impetum ceperat.

p.note: : cf. the epitaph written by Verginius Rufus for his own tomb: Hic situs est Rufus, pulso qui Vindice quondam | imperium asseruit non sibi sed patriae (Plin. Ep. vi 10).

: Trachmann (De conjunctionum causalium ap. Suet. usu, p. 41) says, "Verba 'quippe subirent' ad praecedentia 'desperatione ulla aut diffidentia' ita spectant, ut 'quippe residuis integrisque venientibus aliis' referenda sint ad vocem 'desperatione, verba victis quidem adeo afflictis (sc. et quippe ne quidem)' ad vocem ‘diffidentia.' Itaque duo membra enuntiati ex 'quippe' suspensi ἀσυνδετικῶς posita sunt.” et super- 'ne residuis integrisque (copiis): the strong force which he had taken with him when he withdrew to Brixellum before the battle of Betriacum.

: the meaning seems to be that given by Beroaldus, “Noluit Otho primo discrimini casuique bellico committere copias omnes, sed partem militum sibi reservaverat ad fortunam bellicam, casumque secundo tentandum.” Baumg.-Cr. and the Thes. Ling. Lat. cite this as an example of secundus = felix, which is unsatisfactory. Bentley would alter either secundos to adversos or casus to iactus.

p.mentioned: aliis e Dalmatia Pannoniaque et Moesia
p.note: : cf. Tac. ii 44, Praetorianus miles non virtute se sed proditione victum fremebat. Ne Vitellianis quidem incruentam fuisse victoriam, pulso equite, rapta legionis aquila; superesse cum ipso Othone militum quod trans Padum fuerit; venire Moesiacas legiones; magnam exercitus partem Bedriaci remansisse: hos certe nondum victos, et si ita ferret, honestius in acie perituros: ib. c. 46, Nec praetoriani tantum, proprius Othonis miles, sed praemissi e Moesia eandem obstinationem adventantis exercitus, legiones Aquileiam ingressas nuntiabant, ut nemo dubitet potuisse renovari bellum atrox, lugubre, incertum victis et victoribus. We are told in Tac. ii 11 that two legions (vii Galbiana and xiii Gemina) from Pannonia and two (xi Claudia and xiv Gemina Martia Victrix) from Dalmatia were moving to the support of Otho, and that 2000 men from each of them had been sent on in advance. It is not clear what portion of these forces had arrived in time to take part in the battle of Betriacum (Spooner, Tac. Hist. Introd. pp. 75, 79). From Moesia three legions (iii Gallica, vii Claudia, viii Augusta) or three detachments of them (see Vesp. 6, 2 and notes) had come by the passes of the Julian Alps and had reached (or were approaching) Aquileia, when they received news of the defeat and death of Otho.

: the eagerness of Otho's defeated forces for another encounter is described in Tac. ii 46, Non expectavit militum ardor vocem imperatoris. Bonum haberet animum iubebant: superesse adhuc novas vires et ipsos extrema passuros ausurosque. Neque erat adulatio: ire in aciem, excitare partium fortunam furore quodam et instinctu flagrabant. Plutarch (Oth. 15) says that it was not wonderful that Otho's friends should have done their best to encourage him, but the passionate affection of his soldiers passed all belief (τὸ δὲ τῶν στρατιωτῶν πάθος ἅπασαν ὑπερέβαλε πίστιν); not one of them deserted him to go over to the victors.

: all the MSS., except M, have the reading “Lenis." Macé (Essai sur Suétone, p. 31 sq.) points out that if "Lenis” were what Suetonius wrote, the origin of "Laetus” would be inexplicable; "Laetus,” on the other hand, would easily be corrupted into "Lenis," the successive stages being LAETVS, LETVS, LENS, LENIS; it would also be felt that "Lenis," as a cognomen for the father, corresponded with "Tranquillus," the cognomen of the son.

: Mommsen's view that the 13th legion (Gemina) was created by Augustus in 6 A.D. is rejected by Parker (Roman Legions p. 78 sqq.) and Ritterling (in Pauly-Wissowa xii 1711). After the disaster to Varus in 9 A.D. it was brought (perhaps from Illyricum) to Vindonissa (Windisch) in Upper Germany. Under Claudius (in 45 or 46) it was transferred to Pannonia, whence it came to support Otho (see on c. 9, 3). It was defeated at Betriacum by the 5th legion (Alaudae), the legionaries attributing their defeat to their legatus Vedius Aquila (Tac. H. ii 43 sq.). Vitellius, after his victory, put it to the forced labour of building amphitheatres at Cremona and Bononia (Tac. ii 67, iii 32). It was then sent back to its quarters at Poetovio in Pannonia, but was immediately recalled to support Vespasian, and took part in the victory at Cremona over the Vitellians (Tac. iii 1, 21, 27, 32), after which it was sent back to Pannonia.
: i.e. a tribune of equestrian birth; see on ''tribunus laticlavius,'' Dom. 10, 5. .. deinde ..

: here, as frequently, = post, postea; used in this sense in enumerations also, e.g. Iul. 22, 1, initio. mox: Aug. 19, 1, prima тох exin.. ac praeter has item.. ad extremum: Vitell. 12, тох et rursus iterum deinde: 15, 4, primum..dein. ac mox (cf. Tac. A. xi 22, primum deinde mox post). The generally accepted view that mox for postea is merely post-class. is contested by H. J. Rose, Class. Quart. xxi 2.

: both these leaders of the conspiracy against Julius Caesar perished by the sword. In the first engagement at Philippi (42 в.с.) С. СCassius, hard-pressed and isolated, mistaking for the pursuing foe a force of cavalry which M. Brutus had sent to his support, laid bare his neck and commanded his freedman Pindarus to cut off his head (Plut. Brut. 43); twenty days afterwards, at the second encounter on the same ground, Brutus, routed by Octavius and Antonius, threw himself on his own sword (ib. 52).

: concurrere must be used here in the general sense of opposing, or disputing another's title (certamen de imperio suscipere, Baumg.-Cr.); Burman points out that it cannot bear its more usual meaning of committere proelium, for (1) the statement of Suetonius would be a contradiction, being equivalent to non gesturum fuisse bellum nisi confideret sine bello rem transigi posse; and (2) Otho never did join battle with Galba, he merely won over the praetorians, who gave him the empire and slew Galba. Bentley conjectured occisurum eum Galbam.

: Dio (lxiv 11) tells this story in the same form as Suetonius: ἐπεὶ δὲ οἱ τοῦ ῎Οθωνος ἐκρατήθησαν, ἤγγειλε μὲν ἱππεύς τις τὸ πάθος τῷ Ὄθωνι˙ καὶ ἐπειδή γε ἠπιστεῖτο πρὸς τῶν παρόντων (ἔτυχον γὰρ πολλοὶ κατὰ τύχην ἠθροισμένοι) καὶ οἱ μὲν δραπέτην (fugitivum) οἱ δὲ καὶ πολέμιον αὐτὸν ἀπεκάλουν, “ εἴθε γάρ” ἔφη “ ψευδῆ ταῦτα, Καῖσαρ, ἦν· ἥδιστα γὰρ ἂν νικῶντός σου ἐτελεύτησα. νῦν δὲ ἐγὼ μὲν πάντως οἰχήσομαι, ἵνα μή μέ τις ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ καταπεφευγέναι δόξῃ, σὺ δὲ βουλεύου, ὡς τῶν πολεμίων οὐκ ἐς μακρὰν ἡξόντων, ὅ τι χρὴ πρᾶξαι.” καὶ ὁ μὲν ταῦτ᾽ εἰπὼν ἑαυτὸν διεχρήσατο. Plutarch (Oth. 15) says that the incident occurred when the soldiers after the defeat at Betriacum were imploring Otho not to leave them but to use, as long as there was life in them, their souls and bodies in his service: Εἷς δὲ τῶν ἀφανεστέρων ἀνατείνας τὸ ξίφος καὶ εἰπών “Ἴσθι, Καῖσαρ, οὕτως ὑπὲρ σοῦ παρατεταγμένους (prepared to die) ἅπαντας” ἀπέσφαξεν ἑαυτόν. Tacitus (H. iii 54) tells a similar story of Julius Agrestis, a centurion in the army of Vitellius, who persuaded Vitellius to allow him to go and ascertain the extent of the disaster which their army had sustained at Cremona against Vespasian's forces, and when he brought back his report of the losses incurred, Vitellius refused to believe him and charged him with having been bribed, whereupon Agrestis: quandoquidem” inquit “magno documento opus est, nec alius iam tibi aut vitae aut mortis meae usus, dabo cui credas." Atque ita digressus voluntaria morte dicta firmavit. ..

: cf Tac. ii 47, hunc animum, hanc virtutem vestram ultra periculis obicere nimis grande vitae meae pretium puto: Eutrop. vii 17, petentibus militibus, ne tam cito de belli desperaret eventu, cum tanti se non esse dixisset, ut propter eum bellum civile moveretur, etc. Tacitus (l.c.), Plutarch (Oth. 15), and Dio (lxiv 13) all put into the mouth of Otho a last speech in which he refuses to yield to the entreaties of his soldiers who implored him to continue the struggle; he points out to them that by dying he will benefit the State more than by continuing to live, and that his death will be a glorious death, if by it are ended the horrors of civil strife. Hardy (on Plut. l.c.) says "No doubt all these speeches are inventions of the authors themselves"; but we may be sure that Otho took leave of his men in a speech on some such lines as these.

div.p: § 2. fratrem: Lucius Salvius Otho Titianus; see on c. 1, 3. fratris filium: Lucius Salvius Otho Cocceianus (or Cocceius, Κοκκήϊος Plut.), who was spared by Vitellius, but was put to death by Domitian, nearly 20 years afterwards, for keeping the birthday of his uncle the emperor Otho; see Dom. 10, 3. Plutarch (Oth. 16) describes how Otho bade his nephew have no fear of Vitellius whose family he himself had preserved unhurt; he tells him that he had intended to adopt him as his son but postponed it from considerations of his safety, and he gives him a last warning neither to forget nor to be too mindful of the fact that his uncle had been a Caesar (μήτε ἐπιλαθέσθαι παντάπασι μήτε ἄγαν μνημονεύειν, ὅτι Καίσαρα θεῖον ἔσχες). Cf. Tac. ii 48, Mox Salvium Cocceianum, fratris filium prima iuventa, trepidum et maerentem ultro solatus est, laudando pietatem eius, castigando formidinem: an Vitellium tam inmitis animi fore, ut pro incolumi tota domo ne hanc quidem sibi gratiam redderet? Mereri se festinato exitu clementiam victoris: non enim ultima desperatione, sed poscente proelium exercitu, remisisse rei publicae novissimum casum. Satis sibi nominis, satis posteris suis nobilitatis quaesitum. Post Iulios Claudios Servios se primum in familiam novam imperium intulisse. Proinde erecto animo capesseret vitam, neu patruum sibi Othonem fuisse aut oblivisceretur umquam aut nimium meminisset.

p.note: : Tac. (l.c.), Talia locutus, ut cuique aetas aut dignitas, comiter appellatos, irent propere neu remanendo iram victoris asperarent, iuvenes auctoritate, senes precibus movebat, placidus ore, intrepidus verbis, intempestivas suorum lacrimas coercens. Dari naves ac vehicula abeuntibus iubet.
: see on c. 6, 2. secreto: see on c. 3, 1.
: the distributive numeral, because codicilli is one of the words regularly used in the plural only.

: thin tablets of wood (codices, caudices) covered with wax, used for notes or hasty jottings with a stilus. The word can denote either the tablets or the writing on them; e.g. Cic. Fam. ix 26, harum (litterarum) exemplum in codicillos exaravi: Sen. Ep. 55, adeo tecum sum, ut dubitem, an incipiam non epistulas sed codicillos tibi scribere. See also Marquardt, Privatl. p. 804.

: exarare, “to plough up," was used metaph. of the furrows traced in the wax by the stilus. Cicero uses it freely, but only in his Letters; Suetonius uses it also in Ner. 52, versus quasi a cogitante atque generante exaratas: vit. Lucan., codicillos ad patrem exaravit. .. ..
: see c. 1, 3, where she is mentioned as betrothed to Drusus, son of Germanicus. His

: Statilia Messalina, granddaughter of T. Statilius Taurus (cons. 11 A.D.), and probably daughter of T. Statilius Taurus (cons. 44 A.D.) who was a grandson of the orator Messala (see Prosop. Imp. Rom. iii 266). She was the third of Nero's wives, being married to him c. 66 A.D. previous wives were Octavia and Poppaea. After Poppaea's death, caused by his own brutality (see on c. 3, 1), he wished to marry Antonia, daughter of the emperor Claudius, and when she refused he put her to death. He then selected Messalina, and as she was already married to Atticus Vestinus (cons. 65 A.D.) he had her husband put to death merely for having knowingly married one who numbered Nero among her paramours (Tac. A. xv 68 sq., Suet. Ner. 35). The Schol. on Juv. vi 434, where the poet satirizes literary ladies, says that the accomplished Messalina is aimed at: “Statiliam Messalinam significat, quae post quattuor matrimonia diverso exitu soluta postremo Neroni nupsit; post quem interemptum et opibus et forma et ingenio plurimum viguit. Consectata est usum eloquentiae usque ad studium declamandi. Illo tempore duae Messalinae fuerunt, haec et Valeria de qua Claudius Britannicum filium sustulit." For coins with her name and image see Cohen, i² p. 316; Eckhel, vi 287 sq.

: sc. uxorem. In expressing relationship the appellative nouns (uxor, filius, etc.) are at times omitted as in Greek. This is most frequent in poetry and post-Aug. prose, but there are a few instances in Cicero (Kühner-Stegmann, i 414).

: Tac. ii 48, libellos ("petitions'') epistulasque studio erga se aut in Vitellium contumeliis insignes abolet (= concremat): Zonar. xi 15, τά τε γράμματα ὅσα τινὲς αὐτῷ κατ᾿ ἐκείνου ἐγεγράφεσαν ἔκαυσεν, ὥστε μηδένα ἐξ αὐτῶν φωραθέντα κινδυνεῦσαι, καὶ καλῶν ἕνα ἕκαστον τῶν παρόντων ἠσπάζετο αὐτοὺς καὶ ἐδίδου σφίσι χρήματα. For quicquid c. gen. see on Galb. 1.

: Tacitus (who does not specify to whom the money was given) says that he distributed it sparingly and not like a man about to die: pecunias distribuit parce nec ut periturus. Plutarch (Oth. 17) states that he carefully rewarded each servant according to his deserts, not squandering the money lavishly merely because he knew that it would soon be another's: τοὺς οἰκέτας προσεκαλεῖτο, καὶ φιλοφρονούμενος διένεμε τῶν χρημάτων τῷ μὲν πλέον, τῷ δὲ ἔλαττον, οὐχ ὥσπερ ἀλλοτρίων ἀφειδῶν, ἀλλὰ τὸ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν καὶ τὸ μέτριον ἐπιμελῶς φυλάττων. According to Plut. it was not till later in the evening, after he had chosen the dagger with which to slay himself (see Suet. c. 11, 2), that he made this distribution of money to his servants.

: Tac. ii 49, Post quae, dimotis omnibus, paulum requievit. Atque illum, supremas iam curas animo volutantem, repens tumultus avertit, nuntiata consternatione ac licentia militum: namque abeuntibus exitium minitabantur: Plut. (Oth. 16), Γενόμενος δὲ ἀπὸ τούτων μετὰ μικρὸν ἤκουσε θορύβου καὶ βοῆς ἐπὶ θύραις. Οἱ γὰρ στρατιῶται τῶν συγκλητικῶν (senatorum) τοῖς ἀπιοῦσι διηπείλουν ἀποσφάξειν, εἰ μὴ παραμενοῦσιν, ἀλλ᾽ οἰχήσονται τὸν αὐτοκράτορα (Imperatorem) καταλιπόντες.

: the same phrase is used in Ner. 49, 2, where Nero is hesitating to slay himself and a letter arrives stating that he has been proclaimed a public enemy: inter moras perlatos a cursore Phaonti codicillos praeripuit legitque se hostem a senatu iudicatum.

: this verb only here in Suet.; twice in Cic. (Fin. v 24, Arat. 131); most frequent in poets and Tac. For the use of "frequentative forms by Suet. see App. I § 7. b. detineri: the soldiers were extreme in their violence against Verginius Rufus, whose house they blockaded and besieged: Tac. ii 49, atrocissima in Verginium vi, quem clausa domo obsidebant. Verginius, the conqueror of Vindex (Galb. 9, 2), had been appointed by Otho to be consul suffectus for the year. After Otho's death the soldiers tumultuously demanded that he should undertake the empire, but he managed to slip away from them: Tac. ii 51, per aversam domus partem furtim digressus inrumpentes frustratus est.

: these words, in which Otho announced the postponement of his death for a few hours, are not mentioned by Tacitus or Plutarch. Cf. Hor. C. iv 7, 17, Quis scit an adiciant hodiernae crastina summae (al. vitae) Tempora di superi? his ipsis totidemque verbis: totidem verbis is often used of copies or translations "word for word"; e.g. Cic. Att. vi 2, istum ego locum totidem verbis a Dicaearcho transtuli: Fin. ii 100, totidem verbis interpretari. The emphasis which Suetonius lays on the accuracy of his statement of Otho's words may be due to a desire to correct some current misrepresentation of them. vetuit vim cuiquam fieri: cf. Tac. c. 49, increpitis seditionis auctoribus regressus vacavit abeuntium adloquiis, donec omnes inviolati discederent. Plutarch (Oth. 16) describes how Otho sternly quelled the disorder: πάλιν οὖν προῆλθεν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀνδρῶν φοβηθείς, καὶ τοὺς στρατιώτας οὐκέτι δεητικὸς οὐδὲ πρᾷος, ἀλλὰ τραχὺς ὀφθεὶς καὶ μετ᾿ ὀργῆς εἰς τὸ θορυβοῦν μάλιστα διαβλέψας ἀπελθεῖν ἐποίησεν εἴξαντας καὶ διατρέσαντας.

: cf. Tib. 40, potestatem omnibus adeundi sui fecit: ib. 34, 2, qui potestatem sui die festo non habuissent: Cic. Q. Fratr. i 2, cum neque praetores diebus aliquot adiri possent vel potestatem sui facerent. •

div.p: §2. sedata siti potione: Tac. c. 49, vesperascente die sitim haustu gelidae aquae sedavit: Plut. c. 17, ἤδη δὲ ἑσπέρας οὔσης ἐδίψησε, καὶ πιὼν ὀλίγον ὕδατος, κ.τ.λ.

p.note: : Tac. (l.c.), tum adlatis pugionibus < duobus >, cum utrumque pertemptassset, alterum capiti subdidit. Plutarch says the test took some time: δυεῖν ὄντων αὐτῷ ξιφῶν, ἑκατέρου κατεμάνθανε τὸ σπάσμα (i.e. the blade drawn from the scabbard) πολὺν χρόνον. Similarly Nero, when he heard that he was to be punished "more maiorum,” tested the edges of two daggers: Ner. 49, 2, conterritus duos pugiones, quos secum extulerat, arripuit temptataque utriusque acie rursus condidit, causatus nondum adesse fatalem horam.
: cf. Dom. 17, 2, pugionem subditum pulvino.

: this use of adopertus in the sense of clausus (its normal meaning being tectus, obvolutus velamine quodam) is found earlier only in Ov. Met. i 713, vidit succubuisse oculos adopertaque lumina. somno.

: cf. Aug. 16, 1, arto repente somno devinctus: Cic. Rep. 6, 10, те artior, quam solebat, somnus complexus est. Tacitus (c. 49) puts it less strongly: noctem quietam, utque adfirmatur, non insomnem egit; Plutarch (c. 17) agrees with Suet.: ἀποπέμψας δὲ τούτους ἤδη τὸ λοιπὸν ἀνεπαύετο τῆς νυκτός, ὥστε τοὺς κατευναστὰς (cubicularios) αἰσθάνεσθαι βαθέως αὐτοῦ καθεύδοντος. Cf. the description given by Pliny (Ep. vi 16, 13) of the deep sleep of his uncle, Pliny the Elder, during the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 A.D.: Tum se quieti dedit, et quievit verissimo quidem somno. Nam meatus animae (‘his snoring'") ab iis qui limini obversabantur (i.e. the cubicularii) audiebatur. ..

: circa is used only of place (and that rarely) in Cic. and Caes.; from Livy onwards it is used of time as well, e.g. Suet. Claud. 7, circa initia imperii: Iul. 88, circa undecimam horam; also of number "about" (= ad, circiter), e.g. Claud. 6, 2, circa sestertium vicies. For other uses see on Tit. 4, 3; Dom. 3, 2.

: Dio lxiv 15, ξιφίδιον λαβὼν ἑαυτὸν διεχρήσατο : Mart. vi 32, 4, et fodit certa pectora tota manu. Tacitus (c. 49) says that he fell with his breast upon the steel: Luce prima in ferrum pectore incubuit. Plutarch (c. 17) gives fuller details. He describes how when Otho awoke he sent a freedman to enquire about the senators, and when he returned and said that they had all departed safely, Otho bade him go and show himself to the soldiers that they might not afterwards slay him for having helped to cause his death (as Epaphroditus aided Nero in his suicide, see on Dom. 14, 4). As soon as the freedman had gone, Otho placed his sword upright, and holding it with both hands threw himself upon it and died with a single groan. irrumpentibus ad primum gemitum: Tac. (l.c.) ad gemitum morientis ingressi liberti servique et Plotius Firmus praetorii praefectus unum volnus invenere. ...

: funerare meaning "to give funeral rites to" is post-Aug. funeratus means "done to death" in Hor. C. iii 8, 7, prope funeratus Arboris ictu. Otho had given orders for his hasty burial to prevent his body being mutilated and made a mock of: cf. Tac. (l.c.), Funus maturatum: ambitiosis ("earnest") id precibus petierat, ne amputaretur caput ludibrio futurum (an indignity inflicted on the corpse of Galba, see Galb. 20, 2). For the simple monument erected over his grave see Vitell. 10, 3.

: this erroneous statement is repeated (as usual) by Eutropius (vii 17): voluntaria morte obiit, trigesimo octavo aetatis anno. Otho was born on Apr. 28, 32 A.D. (see c. 2) and died on Apr. 16 or 17, 69 A.D., so that he lived 37 years, all but 12 or 11 days, as Dio (lxiv 15) accurately states: τοῦτο τὸ τέλος τῷ Ὄθωνι ἐγένετο, ζήσαντι ἑπτὰ καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτη, ἕνδεκα ἡμερῶν δέοντα. Tacitus (ii 49) and [Aurelius Victor] Epit. 7 say that he died in his 37th year; Plutarch (Oth. 18) says more loosely: ἔτη ἑπτὰ καὶ τριάκοντα βιώσας. According to Oudendorp and Baumg.-Cr. the inaccurate statement of Suetonius, that Otho died in his 38th year, is due to a method of calculation by which the year of birth and year of death are both included. There are similar difficulties in the statements of Suetonius with regard to the length of life or length of rule in the case of Galba (see on Galb. 23), Vitellius (see on Vitell. 18), and of Titus (see on Tit. 11).

: this too is accepted by Eutropius (l.c.); Dio (l.c.) says that he reigned 90 days; Plutarch (l.c.) 3 months; Josephus (Bell. Iud. iv 9,9) 92 days. Galba was slain on Jan. 15 and Otho's reign began on that day, but there is no means of fixing definitely the day in April on which he died. Opinion is divided between the 15th (so Schiller, Gesch. röm. Kaiserzeit), the 16th (so Krauss, De vitarum imp. Othonis fide quaestiones), and the 17th (so Puhl, De Oth. et Vit. imp. quaest.). Nagl (in Pauly-Wissowa, i A. 2053) strongly favours the 16th, and points out in support of this date that Tacitus (H. ii 55) says that news of Otho's death was brought into the theatre at Rome during the celebration of the Ludi Cereales (Apr. 13-19). On the last day (Apr. 19) of the Ludi Cereales there were games in the Circus, and if the news arrived on that day it would have been brought to the Circus, not to the theatre. The news probably reached Rome late on the 18th, and it was not till the following day that the senate formally appointed Vitellius as emperor (cf. Henzen Act. Fratr. Arv. p. xciv, “ob diem imperi [Vitelli] Germanici imp. quod xiii K. Mai. statutum est"). Allowing 2 days for the message to arrive from Brixellum (367 Roman miles from Rome), Otho died on the 16th, and the battle of Betriacum took place on the 14th (cf. Holzapfel, Klio xiii 289 sqq.). If we assume then that Otho died on Apr. 16, he died on the 92nd day of his reign; Suetonius, who says that he died on the 95th, apparently reckoned from Jan. 15 (date of Otho's accession) to Apr. 19 (date of Vitellius' accession).

: competit is a contracted perf., like petit, c. 7, 1. Suetonius uses competere absolutely in Aug. 31, 3, si cuiusquam neptium suarum competeret aetas (i.e. if any of them were of eligible age for the post of Vestal); in Iul. 40, 1, it takes the abl. (according to the best MSS.): fastos.. adeo turbatos, ut neque messium feriae aestate (v.l. aestati) neque vindemiarum autumno competerent. The dat. is the normal constr. with competere in the sense of "congruere, consentire, convenire, aptum esse"; cf. Nonius (276 M., 424 Lindsay), conpetere, par esse vel simile. unde et in aestimatione rerum “hoc illi conpetit” dicimus.
: see on Galb. 21.

: "ill-set on his feet" ("splay-footed," Clarke). pedatus (ὑπόπους) is not applied to persons elsewhere; the verb is used metaph. of vines in the sense of suffulcire; Colum. iv 12, vineae pedandae cura: Plin. N.H. xvii 164, vineae pedatae simplici iugo. scambus: i.e. with the legs bent out and the feet bent in, bow-legged, bandy-legged. This seems to be the only place where the late Gr. word σκαμβός is found in Latin. The usual word is varus; cf. Varr. R.R. ii 9, (canes) debent esse cruribus rectis et potius varis quam vatiis, which is rendered by the compiler of the Geoponica (xix 2): σκαμβότερα μᾶλλον ἢ βλαισά. In our passage the MSS. have cambus, which Turnebus altered to scambus. Bonnet (Archiv Lat. Lex. 13, 579) defends cambus as the more correct form. He says it is a Gallic word which became completely Latinised, since it serves as a cognomen of different persons, of whom one is mentioned in an African inscription of 329 A.D. (Ephem. epigr. v p. 179).

: cf. Liv. xxxiv 7, munditiae et ornatus et cultus, haec feminarum insignia sunt, his gaudent et gloriantur, hunc mundum muliebrem appellarunt maiores nostri: Ulp. Dig. xxxiv 2, 25, 10, mundus muliebris est, quo mulier mundior fit; continentur eo specula, matulae, unguenta, etc.: Sall. Iug. 85 (Marius speaking), ex parente meo et ex aliis sanctis viris ita accepi, munditias mulieribus, viris laborem convenire: Claud. Eutrop. ii 336, minimeque viriles | munditiae, compti voltus, onerique vel ipsa | serica (“silken garments"). Juvenal (ii 99) ridicules the mirror (speculum) which Otho carried with him on his campaigns: Ille tenet speculum, pathici gestamen Othonis, | Actoris Aurunci spolium, quo se ille videbat | armatum cum iam tolli vexilla iuberet- | res memoranda novis annalibus atque recenti | historia, speculum civilis sarcina belli (the allusions are to the shield described as “magni gestamen Abantis,” Aen. iii 286, and the spear which Turnus was so proud of having taken from Actor, “Actoris Aurunci spolium,” Aen. xii 94). Seneca (N.Q. i 17) is equally severe on the “sarcinae militares" carried by effeminate Romans: Adeoque omnia indiscreta sunt perversissimis artibus, ut quicquid mundus muliebris vocabatur, sarcinae viriles sint: minus dico, etiam militares. Iam speculum ornatus tantum causa adhibitum, nulli non vitio necessarium factum est.
: cf. Galb. 22, n.

: "peruke.” galericulum is a dimin. of galerum (also galerus and galera) which, like κυνέη, was used for a cap made from an animal's skin with the fur or hair left on it; such caps were worn by country labourers, and rustic warriors (e.g. Aen. vii 688; in Frontin. Strateg. iv 7, 29 galericulum is used for the leather headgear of the velites); they were also worn by athletes to save their hair from the unguents used in wrestling, e.g. Mart. xiv 50 (entitled “Galericulum''), Ne lutet immundum nitidos ceroma capillos, | hac poteris madidas condere pelle comas. Then galerum and galericulum came to mean a peruke or wig made of fine skin with human hair attached; Martial (xii 45) mentions one made of kid, Haedina tibi pelle contegenti | nudae tempora (“brows'') verticemque calvae ("skull") | festive tibi, Phoebe, dixit ille | qui dixit caput esse calceatum (“well-shod"). Such wigs were worn at times as disguises, e.g. by Nero on his nightly escapades, Ner. 26, 1, adrepto pilleo vel galero popinas inibat, and by the notorious Messalina in her debauchery, Juv. vi 120, nigrum flavo crinem abscondente galero. See Marquardt, Privatl.2 603 sq.; Daremberg-Saglio, ii 1452 sq.

: Otho's use of bread-poultices for the face is mentioned as one of his effeminacies by Juvenal (ii 103): Nimirum summi ducis est occidere Galbam | et curare cutem, summi constantia civis | Bebriacis campis spolium adfectare Palati | et pressum in facie digitis extendere panem, | quod nec in Assyrio pharetrata Semiramis orbe, | maesta nec Actiaca fecit Cleopatra carina. Again in Sat. vi 461 sqq. Juvenal ridicules the use of these poultices (cataplasmata) by women to beautify their complexions: Interea foeda aspectu ridendaque multo | pane tumet facies aut pinguia Poppaeana | spirat, etc. [“Рорраеапа" were cosmetics called after Poppaea, wife of Otho and Nero (see Oth. 3), who was so careful of her beauty that she always bathed in asses' milk; some of Otho's effeminate habits may have been due to association with her.] Juvenal compares the removal of the poultices to removing stucco: Tandem aperit vultum et tectoria prima reponit. According to the Schol. on Juv. such poultices served two purposes: (1) ad excandendam (‘brightening, whitening'') cutem; (2) ad tendendam faciem aut cutem magis (a medicamen used to tighten the skin and remove wrinkles was called tentipellium, Fest. p. 364 Müll.). .. ..
: for the irregular consecution of nom. and acc. in "fuisse traditur. male pedatus.. rasitare. consuetum" see note on "dicitur obmurmurasse,” c. 7, 2. Bentley would read consuetus.

: lanugo was the first down of manhood; cf. Aen. x 324, flaventem prima lanugine malas: Juv. xiii 59, primaque par sacrae lanugo senectae. The day on which the lanugo or first beard was shaved was celebrated with sacrifices and rejoicings and the lanugo was dedicated to some god; Nero dedicated his in a box adorned with costly pearls to Jupiter Capitolinus (Ner. 12; cf. Juv. iii 186, Petron. Satyr. 29); Caligula was exceptional: uno atque eodem die togam sumpsit barbamque posuit sine ullo honore (Calig. 10, 1).

: the usual practice was to allow the hair on the face to grow again after the first ceremonial shaving (depositio barbae). The young men at Rome (barbatuli iuvenes, bene barbati) wore whiskers either without a beard or with a beard trimmed short; after the age of 40 it was customary to be clean-shaven. See Daremberg-Saglio, i 669 sq.

: the dative maiori (Gr) appears in all the early editions; maiore (MX) is read by Roth, Preud'homme, and Ihm. It is questionable whether the ablative is defensible; the only parallel seems to be a doubtful passage, Flor. ii 11, 6, alligati (the chained captives) miraculo quodam (quidam, Lipsius) fuere, cum catenas morsibus et ore tentassent. In Plin. N.H. xxvii 11, nec quicquam inter herbas maiore equidem miraculo adspexi, the meaning is prob. "with greater wonderment"; cf. xxxii 4, hoc est maioris miraculi (= hoc magis homines admirantur): xii 1, arbor digna miraculo (= quam admiremur). phrase miraculo esse often occurs, but in it miraculo is clearly the dative. In Cic. Att. v 1, 4, multa mihi maiori stomacho quam ipsi Quinto fuerunt, the MSS. give maiore; Orelli restored maiori, which is now the accepted reading. • The

: Tac. H. ii 49, tulere corpus praetoriae cohortes cum laudibus et lacrimis volnus manusque eius exosculantes. The compound exosculari is stronger than the simple verb and denotes passionate kissing. Plutarch (Oth. 17) describes the wild grief of the soldiers at Otho's death and their self-reproaches for not having guarded him more closely and hindered his dying for them. They took no thought for themselves, though the enemy was close at hand. They arrayed the body in state, and in full armour bore it to the pyre: happy were those fortunate enough to support the bier! Some kissed his wound, some clasped his hand, while others, afar off, prostrated themselves.

: Tac. (l.c.), Quidam militum iuxta rogum interfecere se, non noxa neque ob metum, sed aemulatione decoris et caritate principis: [Aur. Vict.] Epit. 7, (Otho) adeo amabilis militibus propriis, ut plerique, corpore eius viso, suis manibus interierint: Dio lxiv 15, καί τινες ἑαυτοὺς ἐπέσφαξαν αὐτῷ: Plut. (l.c.), ἔνιοι δὲ τῇ πυρᾷ λαμπάδας ὑφέντες ἑαυτοὺς ἀπέσφαξαν. Plut. adds that it was not because they had received any special favour from Otho, or that they feared the victor's vengeance; it would seem that no king or tyrant was ever so passionately fond of ruling as they were of being ruled by Otho. Even after his death their affection for him continued and developed into an ineradicable hatred of Vitellius.
: Tac. (l.c.), ac postea promisce ("among all ranks'') Bedriaci Placentiae aliisque in castris celebratum (= saepius adhibitum) id genus mortis.

: this ante-class. and post-class. use of prae (= propter) in a positive sentence occurs also in Iul. 39, 4; Aug. 65, 2; Tib. 66; Calig. 4; Claud. 10, 2:32. In class. writers prae is used in this sense only with an expressed or implied negative or with vix (Kühner-Stegmann, i 513).

: Plutarch (c. 18) says that those who praised Otho's death were not less in number or in worth than those who blamed his life: ἀπέθανε δὲ Ὄθων... ἀπολιπὼν μὴ χείρονας μήδ᾽ ἐλάττους τῶν τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ ψεγόντων τοὺς ἐπαινοῦντας τὸν θάνατον.

: under the early Empire there was constant talk of the restoration of the old republican form of government, especially after Nero's death (see on Galb. 10, 1). Augustus himself, according to Suet. Aug. 28, twice thought of restoring the republic (de reddenda re publica bis cogitavit) in 27 and 23 B.c.; but, as Shuckburgh says in his note on that passage, all Augustus did in reality was to elaborate the restitution of the forms of the republic so far as was consistent with his own supremacy. Cf. also Claud. 1, 4, where Suetonius says that Drusus Germanicus (brother of Tiberius) made no secret of his intention to revive the republic if ever he should have the power: dissimulasse umquam pristinum se rei p. statum, quandoque posset, restituturum. nec
